name: Londinium first settlement (Cornhill bridgehead)
style_hint: Dense grid of low timber-framed strip buildings with mud-brick/wattle walls, thatch or shingle roofs, gable ends fronting gravelled streets running along the Cornhill ridge from the bridgehead; two-storey at most, no masonry.
notes: Founded c.AD 47-50 (earliest dated timber drain AD 47); burnt in the Boudican revolt AD 60/61 and immediately rebuilt on the same grid. Footprint here is a modelling abstraction of the early core, not a measured building? Extent and orientation ?

name: Roman London Bridge
style_hint: Low timber trestle bridge on driven oak pile clusters and squared timber pier bases, plank deck about 6-8 m wide with simple timber parapets; possibly a stone-piered later phase. Deck sits roughly 5-7 m above low water, landing at Fish Street Hill on the north bank and on the Southwark island bridgehead to the south.
notes: Timber piled bridge built c. AD 50 by the founders of Londinium; probably destroyed in the Boudican revolt (AD 60) and rebuilt. Position approximate - archaeological pier evidence lies slightly downstream (east) of the modern bridge, near Fish Street Hill / Pudding Lane. Length, width, deck height and both dates all highly uncertain (?); the c.400 death date is the conventional end of Roman Londinium, not a recorded demolition (?). A succession of Saxon and Norman timber bridges occupied roughly the same site between c.400 and 1209 and are not separately entered here (?). || from landmark fragment: Crossing lay a few tens of metres downstream (east) of the modern London Bridge, on the Fish Street Hill / Borough High Street axis. Timber pier base excavated at Pudding Lane / Fish Street Hill 1981-85. Span length 320 m ? (Roman Thames was wider and shallower than today); deck width and height ?; abandonment c.AD 400 ? - the bridge decayed rather than being destroyed.

name: Roman amphitheatre, timber phase (Guildhall Yard)
style_hint: Elliptical ring of earth banks revetted with timber posts and planking, wooden bench seating on the banks, a timber arena wall and simple timber-lined entrance passages at the ends of the long axis; sand-strewn oval arena floor with a central drain.
notes: Built AD 70 in wood, immediately outside the north-west of the settled area. Timber-phase dimensions are estimated as slightly smaller than the stone rebuild ?; long-axis bearing ~90 degrees ? (entrances recorded east, west and south).

name: First forum-basilica, Londinium
style_hint: Modest masonry complex on a raised platform: an open gravelled courtyard framed on three sides by colonnaded ranges of shops/offices, closed on the north by a two-storey aisled basilica hall with a raised tribunal apse; ragstone and tile walls, painted render, tiled pitched roofs.
notes: Built c.AD 70-85 (MOLA dating c.78-84), roughly a football pitch in area, 100 x 50 m per Wikipedia. Demolished piecemeal c.AD 90-110 as the second forum rose around it. Height 12 m ?; orientation follows the Roman street grid, taken as ~4 degrees east of north ?

name: Huggin Hill public bath-house
style_hint: Large terraced masonry bath block stepping down the hillside toward the Thames: a run of tall barrel-vaulted halls in ragstone and tile with apsidal ends, arched clerestory windows, hypocaust floors on tile pilae, box-flue tiles in the walls, and vaulted roofs; one of the biggest bath suites in Roman Britain.
notes: Built in the later 1st century (c.AD 70-80), demolished around AD 200. Thought to have extended about 75 m along the former river frontage; the eastern caldarium alone was about 16 x 9 m with a west apse, and a second caldarium about 11 x 8 m with a north apse. Overall depth 32 m ? and height 11 m ?. Remains survive buried under Upper Thames Street and Huggin Hill (scheduled monument 1001981).

name: Southwark mansio (Roman guest-house), Borough High Street
style_hint: Substantial courtyard building: ranges of rooms and corridors on all four sides of a central open court, with a large richly decorated dining room (mosaic floor, painted wall plaster), hypocaust-heated rooms, bath suite and stabling/service wings; ragstone footings with mortared masonry and timber upper walls, tiled roofs, single storey with parts rising to two.
notes: Identified from excavations at 15-23 Southwark Street, 1980-86, and reinforced by the 2022 Liberty of Southwark mosaic and dining-room find just to the south-east. A mansio was an official inn for state couriers, sited by the bridge approach on the road to Canterbury and Dover. Footprint 50 x 45 m ?, height 8 m ?, orientation follows the Roman road alignment ?; dates c.AD 70-120 for the main build with occupation into the later Roman period, so death 300 ?

name: Governor's palace (praetorium), Cannon Street
style_hint: Monumental terraced complex on three descending levels from Cannon Street down to the waterfront: ranges of large state rooms with mosaic floors and painted plaster around courtyards, massive masonry retaining walls between terraces, and on the lowest terrace a formal garden with a long ornamental pool about 55 m long and 10 m wide. Ragstone and tile, tiled roofs, colonnaded fronts.
notes: About 130 x 100 m, running from Cannon Street to the Roman waterfront at Upper Thames Street; excavated 1961-72 under and east of Cannon Street station. Dated AD 80-100 (taken as 85). Peter Marsden's identification as the provincial governor's praetorium is disputed - Perring and Milne doubt the complex was a single unified building ?. Height 12 m ? and end date c.AD 300 ?

name: Cheapside bath-house
style_hint: Compact military-style bath suite: a short linear range of three or four small vaulted rooms (frigidarium, tepidarium, caldarium) with hypocausts, an apsidal hot plunge, an attached furnace room with a stoke-hole, plus a timber-lined well and water tank; plain rendered ragstone with tiled roofs.
notes: Excavated 1955 near Cheapside/Bread Street, just south-east of the Cripplegate fort. Built in the late 1st century (c.AD 90-100) and enlarged in the 2nd; relatively small and on the scale of a military bath-house, so probably for the fort garrison. Exact plan dimensions are not published in the accessible sources - 30 x 18 m and 7 m high are estimates ?; end date 250 ?; location precise to about 50 m ?

name: Second basilica great hall (north range of the forum)
style_hint: Enormous aisled hall running the full width of the forum's north side: tall clerestoried central nave carried on two rows of massive piers, flanked by lower side aisles, a raised apsidal tribunal at the east end and a row of small offices along the north. Three storeys in effective height, ragstone-and-tile walls on 4 m deep foundations, timber-trussed tiled roof.
notes: Length over 150 m (about 167 m, matching the forum's north side) and roughly 52.5 m wide ?; described in popular and MOLA accounts as three storeys high, so 25 m ridge height is an estimate ?. Excavated at Leadenhall Court 1984-86 and again at 85 Gracechurch Street 2024-25. Modelled as a separate mass sitting on the north edge of forum_basilica_2.

name: Second forum-basilica, Londinium (great forum)
style_hint: Vast near-square walled precinct of roughly 2.8 ha: a huge open gravelled piazza (courtyard about 100 x 85 m, Trafalgar Square scale) surrounded by double colonnaded porticoes with ranges of shops and offices two storeys high, closed on the north by the towering basilica hall. Ragstone rubble with tile bonding courses, rendered and painted, imported marble veneers on the principal facades.
notes: 168 x 167 m overall per Wikipedia; construction spread over roughly 30 years from c.AD 90/100 to 120-130; largest building of its type north of the Alps. Demolished c.AD 300 (attributed to reprisals after the Carausian/Allectan revolt). Perimeter-range height 15 m ?; the basilica itself is modelled separately as basilica_2_hall.

name: Roman amphitheatre, stone phase (Guildhall Yard)
style_hint: Elliptical arena 105 x 85 m overall: a ragstone arena wall about 2 m high faced with painted plaster, raked timber seating on earth banks retained by masonry, and tile-and-ragstone vaulted entrance tunnels with timber gate thresholds on the east, west and south. Sand arena floor with a timber-lined central drain; capacity 6,000-7,000.
notes: Overall 105 x 85 m (Historic England scheduling); arena floor roughly 62 x 45 m ?. Rebuilt in stone in the early 2nd century (c.AD 100-125; taken as 120). Went out of use in the later 4th century, taken as c.AD 370 ?. Long-axis bearing 90 degrees ?. Remains lie about 8 m below Guildhall Yard.

name: Cripplegate Roman fort
style_hint: Classic playing-card auxiliary fort: rectangular circuit of ragstone curtain wall about 1.2 m thick backed by an earth rampart, rounded corners with internal corner turrets, interval towers, a V-shaped ditch outside, and twin-arched gates in the middle of each side. Inside, regular rows of long timber barrack blocks, a headquarters building and granaries on a grid of gravelled streets.
notes: About 230 x 215 m (roughly 750 x 705 ft, ~12 acres / 4.9 ha); sources disagree, Wikipedia says 'more than 200 x 200 m', one popular source gives 270 x 220 m ?. Built c.AD 110-120 (range 100-150) for roughly 1,000-1,500 men including the governor's guard. Garrison withdrawn and interior dismantled c.AD 200; its north and west walls were then thickened and doubled in height to serve as part of the new city wall, which is why the walled city has a square notch in its north-west corner. Aligned to the cardinal points ?

name: Cripplegate (north gate of the fort)
style_hint: Military fort gate: twin arched carriageways between two square towers of coursed ragstone, guardrooms at ground level and a covered chamber over the passage carrying the rampart walk; heavier and more austere than the civilian gates.
notes: Coordinates 51.518087 N, 0.0931473 W, between Wood Street and Fore Street on the line of London Wall. Began as the north gate of the Cripplegate fort c.AD 120-150, about eighty years before the rest of the wall, and became a city gate when the fort was absorbed. Rebuilt in the 1490s, demolished 1760. Dimensions ?

name: South-west religious precinct and monumental arch
style_hint: Walled temenos in the south-west of the walled city containing one or more small classical temples on podia with columned porches, entered through a richly carved monumental arch about 8 m high decorated with figures of deities, plus a sculptured 'screen of gods'.
notes: Reconstructed from carved blocks - a monumental arch and a screen of gods - found reused as rubble in the riverside wall at Baynard's Castle in 1974-75, implying a religious precinct nearby that was demolished c.AD 270 when the riverside wall was built. Location, size, height and orientation are all conjectural ?. NOTE: the popular claim of a temple of Diana under St Paul's Cathedral comes from William Camden, was contradicted by Wren, and is rejected by modern archaeologists - it is not included as a structure.

name: Newgate
style_hint: The best-evidenced Roman gate: a double roadway (two arches) between two square flanking guardroom towers built of ragstone with tile bonding courses, the towers projecting north and south of the gate passage; upper chamber linking the wall walk across the arches.
notes: Coordinates 51.5147472 N, 0.1003389 W, on Newgate Street at Old Bailey. Plan confirmed by excavations in 1875, 1903 and 1909 - 'a double roadway between two square flanking guardroom towers'. Probably one of the earliest gates, possibly predating the wall ?. Became Newgate Prison; demolished 1767. Height and tower height ?

name: Aldgate
style_hint: Eastern gate on the Colchester road, reportedly with two rounded/circular flanking towers rather than square ones, a single wide arched carriageway and a chamber above carrying the wall walk.
notes: Coordinates 51 30 48 N, 0 04 40 W, at the corner of modern Duke's Place. A gate spanned the road to Colchester here when the wall was built; the two circular towers are reported but the Roman plan is not securely excavated ?. Rebuilt 1108-1147, 1215 and 1607-09; removed 1761. Dimensions and orientation ?

name: Bishopsgate
style_hint: Principal north-east gate straddling Ermine Street: wide arched carriageway with flanking towers of ragstone and tile, wall walk carried over the arch, facing the open road to Lincoln and York.
notes: Coordinates 51 30 58 N, 0 04 54 W, at the junction of Bishopsgate and Wormwood Street (marked today by a stone bishop's mitre). First built in Roman times as the start of Ermine Street; exact Roman date unrecorded, taken as c.AD 200 ?. Demolished 1760. Dimensions and orientation ?

name: Cripplegate fort walls incorporated into the city wall
style_hint: The fort's original 1.2 m thick west (and north) curtain doubled in height and thickened on the inner face with a second skin of ragstone, producing a visibly two-phase wall with a straight vertical joint - the classic view in the Noble Street ruins.
notes: Represents the west side of the fort, about 230 m long, reused c.AD 200 when the landward city wall was built. Best surviving stretch is on Noble Street and in the London Wall car park (west gate of the fort, Historic England list entry 1018889). Height 6 m ? and combined thickness 3.2 m ?

name: Roman city wall of Londinium (landward circuit)
style_hint: Continuous Kentish ragstone curtain about 2.5-3 m thick at a chamfered plinth, tapering upward, with double or triple bonding courses of flat red tile every ~1 m of height and a rubble-and-mortar core; an earth bank piled against the inner face and a V-shaped berm ditch 2 m deep and 3-5 m wide outside. Wall walk with a crenellated parapet on top; internal turrets added in the 4th century.
notes: Built c.AD 190-225 (commonly 'around AD 200'), about 3.2 km (2 miles) on the landward side, up to 6 m high plus roughly a 2 m parapet, 2.5-3 m thick. Enclosed roughly 130 ha. Never fully destroyed - it stood through the medieval period and fragments survive, so death is null. Given lon/lat is a centroid of the walled area, not a wall point; orientation is meaningless for a closed circuit and is set to 90 as a placeholder ?

name: Ludgate (Roman/medieval gate)
style_hint: Roman gate of a double arched carriageway flanked by two square ragstone-and-tile guard towers projecting forward of the wall face, with a chamber and wall-walk over the arches; parapet and small windows to the towers.
notes: Westernmost gate of the London Wall, at the top of Ludgate Hill where it meets Old Bailey; coordinates 51 30 50.3 N, 0 06 08.2 W. One of the original Roman gates. Rebuilt repeatedly in the medieval period (a debtors' prison) and rebuilt in 1586 (see ludgate) and finally demolished 30 July 1760; this record is closed off at the 1586 rebuild to avoid double-counting the Tudor gate. Dimensions and orientation are typologically estimated ?

name: Temple of Mithras (London Mithraeum), Walbrook
style_hint: Small basilican temple sunk partly below ground to evoke Mithras's cave: a narrow central nave flanked by two raised timber-fronted side benches on seven pairs of columns, a semicircular apse at the west end holding the tauroctony relief, entrance and narthex at the east; ragstone and tile walls, low timber roof, dim interior lit by lamps.
notes: Built c.AD 240 on the east bank of the Walbrook at 12 Walbrook, EC4; coordinates 51 30 45 N, 0 05 26.16 W. Rededicated (probably to Bacchus) in the early 4th century and out of use by c.AD 400 ?. Overall roughly 18 x 8 m as commonly quoted ?; ridge height 7 m ?; long axis approximately east-west with the apse at the west, taken as 80 degrees ?. Excavated 1954, relocated 100 m in 1962, returned to the original site in 2017 seven metres below the Bloomberg building.

name: Roman riverside wall
style_hint: Lower, rougher wall than the landward circuit, built in stages on a raft of oak piles and chalk along the Thames foreshore; ragstone facing over a core packed with reused sculpted masonry - altars, cornices and a monumental arch robbed from demolished public and religious buildings. Roughly 4.5 m high and 2 m thick, with occasional water gates.
notes: Dated c.AD 270-280 by dendrochronology on the oak piles (some sources say begun as early as 250-270; Wikipedia gives 280, repaired c.390). Ran about 1.6 km (a mile) from Blackfriars to Tower Hill, closing the circuit. Height 4.5 m ? and thickness 2 m ?; decayed/robbed after the Roman withdrawal, taken as c.410 ?. Coordinate is a mid-point on the Upper Thames Street line, not a building centre.

name: Aldersgate
style_hint: Single-carriageway gate inserted into an existing wall stretch, with a plain arched passage between two modest rectangular towers of ragstone and tile; less monumental than the first-generation gates.
notes: Coordinates 51.51750 N, 0.09722 W. NOT one of the original Roman gates - added later in the Roman period, conventionally c.AD 350 ?. Demolished 1761. Dimensions, height and orientation are typological estimates ?

name: Westminster Abbey (Edward the Confessor's church)
style_hint: The first great Romanesque church in England, built in the Norman manner before the Conquest: a long aisled nave of about twelve bays with cylindrical piers and round arches, projecting transepts, a low square lantern tower over the crossing, an apsidal east end, and two west towers; as shown in the Bayeux Tapestry, with a weathercock being fixed to the roof.
notes: Rebuilt by Edward the Confessor from c.1042, consecrated 28 December 1065 - eight days before his death. Progressively demolished from 1245 for Henry III's church; only parts of the undercroft, the Pyx Chamber and some cloister walls survive. Dimensions are estimates from excavation and the Bayeux Tapestry? Era label 'Saxon' by date, though the architecture is Norman Romanesque.

name: Baynard's Castle (Norman)
style_hint: Norman motte-less riverside enclosure castle at the mouth of the Fleet: stone curtain with square angle turrets, a squat rectangular keep-like hall block against the north side, ragstone rubble with ashlar dressings, crenellated, water gate onto the Thames foreshore.
notes: Built by Ralph Baynard soon after 1066; razed by King John 14 Jan 1213. Exact position uncertain? - placed roughly 100 m NW of the later (1275+) castle, which Wikipedia locates at 51.51139/-0.10000. Footprint and heights are estimates? - no measured plan survives; the site was sold in 1275 to form the Blackfriars precinct.

name: Montfichet's Tower
style_hint: Small Norman motte-and-bailey stronghold on the Ludgate Hill slope above the Fleet: low earthen motte carrying a square stone tower-keep of two or three storeys with clasping corner pilasters, ringed by a timber-then-stone bailey palisade and ditch.
notes: One of the three Norman fortresses of London (with the Tower and Baynard's Castle), raised by the Montfichet family in the 1070s. Demolished 1213 by King John along with Baynard's Castle; the site was absorbed into the Blackfriars precinct in 1275. All dimensions are estimates? - only fragmentary excavated evidence (Ludgate Hill / Ireland Yard).

name: Bermondsey Abbey (priory church of St Saviour)
style_hint: Cluniac priory (abbey from 1399): cruciform aisled church with a low square crossing tower, apsidal-chapelled east end in the Norman phase, cloister and chapter house on the south side, refectory, infirmary and a large walled precinct running north to the Thames.
notes: Founded 1082 as a Cluniac priory, church begun and dedicated 1089; raised to abbey 1399; surrendered 1538. Church dimensions are estimates informed by excavation around Bermondsey Square? - published excavated plans give an aisled church of roughly 80-90 m.

name: St Mary-le-Bow (medieval)
style_hint: A Norman city church built over a substantial stone-vaulted crypt of groin-vaulted bays on massive piers - the 'bows' or arches that gave the church its name - with an aisled nave above and a west tower; rebuilt and heightened in the later Middle Ages, its bells the ones that define a Cockney.
notes: Built for Lanfranc in the 1080s; the crypt (c.1090) survives and is the oldest parochial building in the City. The tower fell in a storm in 1271 killing about 20 people. Destroyed in the Great Fire 1666. Dimensions and heights are estimates?

name: Old Palace of Westminster
style_hint: A dense, irregular medieval-to-Georgian warren on the riverbank rather than a designed palace: Westminster Hall as the great block on the west, the Painted Chamber and St Stephen's Chapel to its east and south, the Court of Requests, Exchequer, law courts wedged against the hall's west side, cloisters, the Jewel Tower detached to the south-west, and a jumble of later brick and stone additions right up to the Thames wall.
notes: The principal royal residence from Edward the Confessor (c.1042-1050) until the fire of 1512, thereafter the seat of Parliament and the law courts. Almost entirely destroyed by fire on 16 October 1834 (tally sticks burnt in an overheated stove); only Westminster Hall, the crypt and cloisters of St Stephen's, and the Jewel Tower survive. Overall extent is an approximation? - treat as a district, not one building.

name: Westminster Hall
style_hint: The largest medieval hall in Europe with an unsupported roof: an enormous stone box 73 x 20.7 m (floor area about 1547 sq m) with thick Norman side walls refaced with Perpendicular panelling and windows, a great north front with a big traceried window between two turrets, and above it all Hugh Herland's oak hammerbeam roof - 660 tonnes of oak springing from carved angels, with no columns beneath.
notes: Foundations laid 1097 for William Rufus, completed 1099. The hammerbeam roof commissioned by Richard II in 1393 and finished c.1401. Scene of the trials of William Wallace, Thomas More, Guy Fawkes and Charles I, and of coronation banquets and royal lyings-in-state. Survived both the 1834 fire and the 1941 bombing. Floor area 1547 sq m documented; the 73 x 20.7 m figures are the standard quoted dimensions; roof apex height (~28 m / 92 ft) is the conventional figure but not confirmed on Wikipedia?

name: White Tower, Tower of London
style_hint: The great Norman donjon: a nearly cubic keep 36 x 32 m at the base and 27 m to the southern battlements, walls up to 4.6 m thick at the base of Kentish rag and Caen stone, three tall storeys over a basement, square turrets at three corners with a round stair turret at the north-east, a semicircular apse bulging from the south-east for the Chapel of St John, and small round-headed windows (many enlarged by Wren). Onion-domed lead cupolas with weathervanes on the four turrets.
notes: Traditionally begun 1078 for William the Conqueror; dendrochronology suggests 1075-1079, complete by 1100 at the latest. Whitewashed in 1240, hence the name. Footprint (36 x 32 m) and height (27 m) documented on Wikipedia; turret tops about 32 m is an estimate? Orientation about 95 deg (long axis roughly E-W, chapel apse to the east) is an estimate?

name: Holy Trinity Priory, Aldgate
style_hint: The richest Augustinian house in London: cruciform aisled church with crossing tower, 13th-century rebuilt eastern arm, cloister and chapter house south of the nave, large precinct filling the block between Leadenhall Street and Duke's Place.
notes: Founded 1108 by Matilda, queen of Henry I. The FIRST English monastery to be dissolved - surrendered to Henry VIII in 1532, four years before the general suppression - and granted to Sir Thomas Audley, who demolished most of it. A fragment of the church survives embedded in a building in Mitre Street. Dimensions are estimates from excavation and antiquarian plans?

name: St Bartholomew's Hospital (medieval)
style_hint: A loose group of low ragstone and timber ranges around a yard: long open infirmary halls with beds in bays down each side, the hospital church of St Bartholomew-the-Less with a small tower on the west side, a master's house, kitchens and a gate to Smithfield.
notes: Founded 1123 by Rahere with the priory; refounded 1546 by Henry VIII as a City hospital - it has occupied the same site continuously since 1123, the oldest in Britain. The medieval fabric was progressively cleared for the Gibbs rebuild from 1730. Dimensions estimated?

name: St Bartholomew-the-Great priory church
style_hint: Massive Norman work: an apsidal choir with an ambulatory ringed by heavy cylindrical piers and round arches, a triforium above, a crossing and transepts, and originally a long aisled nave running west to the surviving gateway on Little Britain. Only the choir, crossing, transepts and one nave bay remain; a squat brick tower of 1628 stands at the truncated west end.
notes: Founded 1123 by Rahere as an Augustinian priory alongside the hospital. Dissolved 1539; the nave was pulled down and the choir kept as a parish church, so the standing building is roughly the eastern half of the original. Full original length estimated at about 88 m; surviving portion about 40 m? Heights estimated.

name: Winchester Palace, Southwark
style_hint: London town house of the Bishops of Winchester: a first-floor great hall over a vaulted river-access cellar, its west gable pierced by a great rose window over three service doorways; the hall lay between two courtyards with chapel, lodgings, prison (the Clink), brewhouse and a walled garden with tennis court and bowling alley.
notes: Built for Bishop Henry of Blois from the 1130s; the great hall usually dated c.1136 with the rose window and enlargement in the 14th century (possibly under William of Wykeham 1367-98) rather than the 1220s? - dating of the rose window is disputed. Remodelled 1682-86, subdivided into tenements and warehouses c.1700, burnt 1814. The west gable and rose window survive as an English Heritage scheduled monument. Hall dimensions estimated from the surviving gable width?

name: Priory of St John of Jerusalem, Clerkenwell
style_hint: English headquarters of the Knights Hospitaller: originally a circular Romanesque nave (like the Temple) with a long aisled rectangular choir over a barrel-vaulted crypt, rebuilt with a rectangular nave in the 15th century; a walled precinct with prior's lodging, hall, cloister and the 1504 gatehouse to the south.
notes: Founded c.1144, church consecrated 1185 by Heraclius of Jerusalem (the same visit that consecrated the Temple Church). Burnt in the Peasants' Revolt 1381 and rebuilt; dissolved 1540; the choir was blown up with gunpowder in 1549 for building stone. The 12th-century crypt survives beneath the present St John's Church, and the outline of the round nave is marked in St John's Square. Dimensions estimated?

name: Temple Church
style_hint: Two joined volumes: a circular Romanesque nave 55 ft (17 m) across, ringed by six clustered Purbeck marble piers under round arches with a blind-arcaded aisle wall and a west doorway of rich chevron work, and abutting it to the east an Early English 'hall church' chancel of three equal aisles with slender Purbeck shafts and a vault 36 ft 3 in (11.05 m) high. The Templar effigies lie on the round nave floor.
notes: Round nave consecrated 10 February 1185 by Heraclius, Patriarch of Jerusalem; the enlarged chancel consecrated Ascension Day 1240. Gutted by incendiaries in May 1941 and restored 1947-58. Round nave diameter and chancel vault height documented; overall length and external roof height estimated?

name: Kingston Bridge (medieval timber bridge)
style_hint: Timber piled trestle bridge on driven oak piles with a plank deck.
notes: A timber bridge existed at Kingston from at least 1193 and probably earlier; for centuries it was the only Thames crossing between London Bridge and Staines. Described as dangerously decayed in 1318, damaged in the Wars of the Roses, repeatedly patched and eventually condemned in the early 1800s. Birth year 1190 is a nominal date for a bridge first documented in 1193 (?). It stood a short distance downstream of the present bridge, near the mouth of the Hogsmill; coordinates approximate (?). kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category. Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Priory and Hospital of St Mary Spital
style_hint: Augustinian priory-hospital: aisled church on the north with a long aisled infirmary hall running east from it towards a chapel, cloister and canons' ranges to the south, a detached charnel house and open-air pulpit (the Spital Cross) in the churchyard to the north-west; ragstone rubble, tiled roofs.
notes: Founded 1197, refounded 1235, dissolved 1539. Excavated extensively by MOLA (Spitalfields, 1991-2007) - one of the largest medieval cemetery excavations in Europe; the church and infirmary plans are archaeologically recorded but the exact lengths quoted here are estimates from the published plan? Heights are estimates?

name: Old London Bridge
style_hint: A stone bridge of nineteen irregular pointed arches on massive boat-shaped starlings that choked the channel and made the water 'race' through, with a drawbridge and a fortified stone gate at the Southwark end where traitors' heads were displayed on pikes; the roadway only about 4 m wide between continuous four- and five-storey timber-framed houses and shops that overhung the river on both sides and were joined by arches across the road.
notes: Begun 1176 by Peter of Colechurch, completed 1209. Nineteen pointed stone arches on massive timber-piled piers with protective starlings, a central drawbridge (last opened in the 1470s) and the Chapel of St Thomas. Carried houses and shops up to seven storeys until the London Bridge Act 1756; houses demolished 1758-1761 and the two central arches replaced by one 'Great Arch' in 1758-62. Closed and demolished 1831-32 after New London Bridge opened. Sat about 30 m downstream (east) of the modern alignment, on the line of Fish Street Hill; coordinates derived from that offset (?). Deck height above mean water approximate (?). || from landmark fragment: Built 1176-1209 by Peter de Colechurch, replacing timber predecessors - the first stone bridge across the tidal Thames and the only bridge in London until 1750. Houses cleared 1758-62; the bridge was demolished in 1831 when Rennie's new bridge opened about 30 m upstream. Its line lay roughly on Fish Street Hill, just EAST of the present London Bridge. Length about 900 ft (276 m); orientation is nearly N-S across the river.

name: Chapel of St Thomas on London Bridge
style_hint: A two-storey chapel standing on its own enlarged pier in the middle of the bridge, projecting east over the water: an upper chapel entered from the roadway and a lower crypt reached by stairs down to the river, with tall traceried windows, a spirelet or bellcote, and the tomb of the bridge's builder Peter de Colechurch in the undercroft.
notes: Dedicated to St Thomas Becket, the Londoner-born martyr; completed with the bridge in 1209 and rebuilt in Perpendicular style in the 14th century. Suppressed at the Reformation, converted to a house and shop in 1553, demolished 1758-62. Position on the bridge (roughly the ninth pier from the north) and all dimensions are estimates?

name: Old St Paul's Cathedral (Norman)
style_hint: Vast Romanesque cathedral rebuilt after the 1087 fire: a twelve-bay aisled nave with massive cylindrical piers, round arches and a triforium, long transepts, a square central tower, and an apsidal Norman east end; heavy Caen and Reigate stone walls with small round-headed windows and a lead-covered timber roof.
notes: Begun after the fire of 1087 under Bishop Maurice, consecrated 1240 - the longest building campaign of any English cathedral. A timber steeple was erected on the crossing tower in 1221. The Norman east end was replaced from 1256 by the Gothic 'New Work'. Length before the eastward extension is an estimate (~152 m)? Nave vault and tower heights are estimates?

name: Tower of London inner curtain wall and towers
style_hint: The inner ward wall wrapping the White Tower: a taller ring than the outer wall (so archers could shoot over it), Kentish rag with an embattled wall-walk, punctuated by thirteen mural towers - Bell, Beauchamp, Devereux, Flint, Bowyer, Brick, Martin, Constable, Broad Arrow, Salt, Lanthorn, Wakefield and Bloody - mostly round or D-shaped drums of two or three storeys rising a storey or two above the wall-walk. The Wakefield and Lanthorn towers form the royal lodgings on the south, and Tower Green and the King's House lie inside on the west.
notes: Begun under Richard I from about 1190 (Bell Tower, western ditch) and greatly extended by Henry III in the 1220s-1240s, when the ward reached the dimensions it still has. Wall height (~11 m) and tower heights (~18 m) are estimates? - Wikipedia gives no figures. Inner ward dimensions are estimates measured off the plan?

name: Savoy Palace
style_hint: The grandest noble town house of medieval London: a walled riverside precinct between the Strand and the Thames, ranges around two courts, a tall aisleless great hall with louvre, a chapel, an embattled gatehouse to the Strand and a watergate and river stair to the south; stone with tiled roofs.
notes: Land granted to Peter II of Savoy 1246, palace built 1263; hugely enlarged and enriched 1340s-1370s by John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster. Sacked and burnt 13 June 1381 in the Peasants' Revolt and left ruinous. Dimensions are estimates? - no plan survives; reconstructions from Wyngaerde put the river frontage around 90-110 m.

name: Westminster Abbey (Henry III's church)
style_hint: French-inspired High Gothic on an English plan: an apsidal east end with a radiating chevet of chapels, hugely tall proportions with a vault 102 ft (31 m) up - the highest in England - a narrow nave with slender Purbeck shafts, a deep triforium, flying buttresses, and enormous transepts with rose windows north and south; the great octagonal chapter house and the cloister to the south.
notes: Begun 6 July 1245 for Henry III to make a fitting shrine for Edward the Confessor, whose body was translated to the new shrine in 1269. Only the east end, transepts and the first bay of the nave were finished in this campaign. Nave vault 102 ft (31 m) documented; external roof ridge height and overall footprint width across transepts (about 61 m) are estimates? The 161 m length is the completed church, not the 1269 state.

name: Baynard's Castle (1275 relocation)
style_hint: Fortified riverside mansion rebuilt on reclaimed Thames foreshore about 100 m SE of the Norman site: irregular walled enclosure with hall range on the river front, embattled parapet, small angle towers, ragstone.
notes: The Norman site passed to Archbishop Kilwardby in 1275 for the Dominican priory, and the Baynard's Castle name moved to a new house built out over the river. Burnt in a 'great fire' in 1428. All dimensions are estimates?

name: St Thomas's Tower and Traitors' Gate
style_hint: A water-gate range built out over the river frontage: a wide segmental stone arch about 18 m across springing from the moat water (Traitors' Gate), with a timber-framed and stone lodging above containing Edward I's private apartments, twin turrets and an embattled parapet; a small dock behind the arch.
notes: Built 1275-1279 for Edward I as the castle's river entrance, named for the chapel of St Thomas Becket within. Prisoners including Anne Boleyn and the future Elizabeth I were brought in through it, giving it the later name Traitors' Gate. Dimensions estimated?

name: Tower of London outer curtain wall and moat
style_hint: Edward I's concentric outer ring, lower than the inner wall: a continuous embattled curtain with squat semicircular bastions (Legge's Mount, Brass Mount) at the north corners, a river-front range with St Thomas's Tower and Traitors' Gate on the south, and the Byward and Middle Towers guarding the twisting entrance causeway from the west; beyond it a broad tidal moat fed from the Thames.
notes: Built 1275-1285 under Edward I, completing the concentric plan and making the Tower the largest and strongest castle in England. Total castle area 12 acres (4.9 ha) documented, plus 6 acres of Tower Liberties. The moat was drained in 1843 and was originally about 4.5 m deeper in the middle than the present ditch. Wall heights and ward dimensions are estimates measured off the plan?

name: St Etheldreda's, Ely Place
style_hint: The private chapel of the Bishops of Ely's London palace: a tall aisleless two-storey chapel with a stone-vaulted undercroft, an upper chapel reached by a stair, huge Geometric Decorated traceried windows east and west, no tower; set back behind a courtyard off Ely Place.
notes: Built c.1284-1290 for Bishop William de Luda. One of only two surviving buildings in London from Edward I's reign; the rest of Ely Palace (with its famous strawberry gardens, referenced in Richard III) was demolished 1772. Returned to Roman Catholic use 1874; roof and glass rebuilt after 1940s bomb damage. Dimensions estimated?

name: Eleanor Cross, Charing
style_hint: The grandest of the twelve Eleanor crosses: a stepped octagonal base carrying three diminishing tiers - an open arcaded stage with statues of Queen Eleanor under crocketed gables, a blind traceried stage, and a tall pinnacled finial with a cross; Caen stone, richly carved.
notes: Made 1291-94 by order of Edward I, by the mason Richard of Crundale, marking the last overnight stop of Eleanor of Castile's funeral procession. Pulled down 1647 by order of Parliament. Its site is where the equestrian statue of Charles I now stands at the top of Whitehall - the point from which distances to London are measured. Height is an estimate? - it was the largest and most expensive of the series, so likely 12-14 m.

name: Old St Paul's Cathedral (Gothic, with spire)
style_hint: The largest building in medieval Britain: 586 ft (179 m) long and 88 m across the transepts, a Norman nave running west and a soaring Gothic 'New Work' choir to the east with a great rose window, all crowned by a square crossing tower carrying an immensely tall lead-covered timber spire topped by a gilt ball and cross. A great cross-shaped mass with lead roofs, flying buttresses on the east arm, and Paul's Cross preaching cross in the churchyard to the north-east.
notes: Gothic eastward extension ('New Work') 1256-1314; spire completed c.1310 and traditionally 489 ft (149 m) high - the tallest spire ever built until Lincoln, and one of the tallest structures in the world at the time. Wren estimated 460 ft and Hooke measured the stone tower at 204 ft (62 m) with the timber spire about the same again above, giving ~408 ft (124 m) - so the height is genuinely disputed? The spire was struck by lightning and burnt on 4 June 1561 and never rebuilt. Nave vault height (~28 m) and external ridge (~39 m) are estimates?

name: Blackfriars (Dominican) Priory
style_hint: Large Dominican precinct in the SW angle of the city wall: an aisled preaching nave separated by a walking-place from a long aisleless choir, no big tower (a small bell-cote only), great cloister to the south with chapter house, frater and dormitory, and a second court; the whole enclosed by a wall taken down to the Thames and the Fleet.
notes: The friars moved here in 1276 onto the sites of Baynard's Castle and Montfichet's Tower; the city wall was rerouted for them. Parliaments met here, and the legatine court that tried Henry VIII's first divorce sat here in 1529. Dissolved 1538. Church dimensions from excavated evidence but quoted figures vary? Height estimated?

name: Greyfriars (Franciscan) Priory church, Newgate
style_hint: One of the largest churches in medieval London: a vast aisled preaching hall of eleven bays plus choir, deliberately towerless in Franciscan fashion, with slender piers, huge traceried windows and a single continuous roof; cloister, library and friars' ranges to the north, precinct running to Newgate Street.
notes: Friars arrived 1225; the great church was built 1306-1348, largely paid for by Queen Margaret and Queen Isabella, both buried here. About 300 ft (91 m) long - second only to Old St Paul's in the City. Dissolved 1538; the church became the parish church of Christ Church Newgate Street, and Christ's Hospital school occupied the claustral buildings. Burnt in the Great Fire 1666. Length is well attested but width and height are estimates?

name: St Stephen's Chapel, Palace of Westminster
style_hint: A two-storey royal chapel modelled on the Sainte-Chapelle: an upper chapel for the king with immensely tall traceried windows, painted and gilded walls, a vaulted timber ceiling and octagonal stair turrets at the corners, standing over a lower chapel (St Mary Undercroft) with a low stone vault; a cloister on the north side.
notes: Begun 1292 for Edward I, finished under Edward III c.1348; from 1548 to 1834 the upper chapel was the debating chamber of the House of Commons, which is why the Commons still has facing benches (the old choir stalls). Destroyed in the fire of 16 October 1834; the crypt and cloister survive. Dimensions commonly quoted as about 90 x 30 ft with the vault around 90 ft up? - not confirmed on Wikipedia, treat as estimates.

name: Whitefriars (Carmelite) Priory
style_hint: Carmelite friary between Fleet Street and the Thames: aisled preaching nave and long choir under one roof line, no tower, cloister and prior's lodging to the south, a vaulted undercroft beneath the prior's house, precinct walls running down to a river stair.
notes: Founded 1247, church largely rebuilt in the 14th century, dissolved 1538. The precinct became the 'Alsatia' sanctuary district. A small 14th-century vaulted crypt (probably the prior's undercroft) survives under Britton's Court, off Whitefriars Street. Church dimensions and heights are estimates?

name: Austin Friars priory church
style_hint: Great Augustinian friary church of preaching-box type: a wide six-bay aisled nave with no clerestory tower, a slender lead-covered spire on a small tower over the junction, and a long aisled choir to the east; cloister, chapter house and dormitory ranges to the north; large precinct with gardens between Throgmorton Street and London Wall.
notes: Founded c.1260-1265 by Humphrey de Bohun; the great church largely rebuilt from 1354. Its spire was one of the landmarks of the medieval City skyline (spire height estimated? - it was destroyed in a storm and rebuilt, finally lost in a 1633 fire). Dissolved 1538 and granted to William Paulet, who demolished the choir and transepts. Nave and choir lengths estimated?

name: London Charterhouse (Carthusian priory)
style_hint: Carthusian plan, unlike any other London house: a very large square great cloister (roughly 100 m a side) ringed by about 25 detached two-storey monks' cells, each with its own walled garden and hatch; a comparatively small aisleless church with a low tower on the south side, plus chapter house, prior's cell and an outer service court.
notes: Founded 1371 by Sir Walter Manny on a Black Death burial ground. Its prior John Houghton and several monks were executed in 1535 for refusing the Oath of Supremacy; suppressed 1537. Great cloister size documented by excavation and the surviving cell doorways; church and tower dimensions estimated?

name: Southwark Cathedral (St Mary Overie priory church)
style_hint: Cruciform Gothic priory church: an aisled nave of six bays, a square crossing tower with four corner pinnacles, short transepts, a five-bay aisled choir with a retrochoir of four parallel aisles at the extreme east end; Kentish ragstone, big Early English lancets in the retrochoir, Perpendicular tower top.
notes: The first Gothic church in London: rebuilt from 1220 after a fire, the work continuing to about 1420. Priory dissolved 1539; parish church of St Saviour thereafter; the decayed medieval nave was demolished 1839 and rebuilt by Arthur Blomfield 1890-97 in 13th-century manner; became a cathedral in 1905. Length about 289 ft and tower about 163 ft are the conventional figures but not confirmed on Wikipedia? Nave height estimated.

name: Baynard's Castle (Duke of Gloucester's palace)
style_hint: Four ranges in a trapezoidal plan around a courtyard, its long south front standing directly out of the Thames with five projecting semi-octagonal river towers; three storeys of brick and stone, mullioned windows, embattled parapets, tall stacks. A second courtyard was added to the west c.1550 by the Earl of Pembroke.
notes: Rebuilt after the 1428 fire by Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester; remodelled as a royal palace by Henry VII c.1501; Pembroke extension c.1550. Edward IV and Richard III were both offered the crown here, and Lady Jane Grey's council met here. Destroyed in the Great Fire 1666; one round tower survived to c.1720. Dimensions estimated from Wyngaerde's panorama and the Agas map? - the river front is usually reconstructed at 80-90 m.

name: Guildhall, City of London
style_hint: The City's civic great hall: a vast stone-vaulted-crypt-on-two-levels supporting a single aisleless hall of about 152 x 49 ft, with tall Perpendicular windows, clustered wall shafts, banners and a high open timber roof; entered through an elaborate south porch. George Dance's 1788 south front is a strange 'Hindoostani Gothic' composition of ogee arches and pinnacles.
notes: Built 1411-1440 under John Croxton - the only stone secular building in the City to survive the Great Fire, though its roof was burnt in 1666 (replaced with a flat roof 1670). Horace Jones's 1866 roof was destroyed in the raid of 29/30 December 1940; Giles Gilbert Scott's present roof dates from 1954. Hall dimensions of about 152 x 49 ft and roof apex about 89 ft are the conventional figures but are not confirmed on Wikipedia? Long axis runs roughly north-south.

name: Lollards' Tower, Lambeth Palace
style_hint: A tall square river-front tower of Kentish ragstone, five storeys with small square-headed windows, a projecting stair turret and an embattled parapet; attached to the west end of the chapel, with a timber-lined prison room at the top.
notes: Built 1435-1440 for Archbishop Chichele. Traditionally a lock-up for Lollard heretics - the top room retains eight iron rings and graffiti - though the association is partly legend? Dimensions estimated?

name: Bella Court, Greenwich
style_hint: Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester's riverside pleasure house: a moderate courtyard house of brick and stone with a great hall, a chapel and a celebrated library, set in an enclosed park with a hilltop tower (Duke Humphrey's Tower, later the site of the Royal Observatory).
notes: Begun after Humphrey was granted the manor in 1427, built from the 1430s and named Bella Court; seized 1447 by Margaret of Anjou, who renamed it Placentia ('pleasant place'). Rebuilt by Henry VII from 1498. Dimensions estimated?

name: Crosby Hall, Bishopsgate (original site)
style_hint: The great hall of a rich merchant's courtyard mansion: a tall single-volume hall of stone with a two-storey oriel bay, large Perpendicular transomed windows, a moulded stone cornice, and a spectacular timber roof of arched braces with pendant hammerbeams and a central octagonal louvre.
notes: Built 1466-1475 for the wool merchant Sir John Crosby on land leased from St Helen's Priory; described by Stow as the highest house in London. Richard III used it as his London base; Sir Thomas More owned it 1523-24. Dismantled from Bishopsgate in 1908-10. Hall dimensions usually given as about 69 x 27 ft with a roof about 40 ft high? - not confirmed in the Wikipedia text.

name: Eltham Palace great hall
style_hint: Edward IV's great hall: a tall ragstone hall of about 100 x 36 ft with big Perpendicular transomed windows, a projecting oriel at the dais end, a stone-flagged floor and one of the finest false-hammerbeam roofs in England; approached across a stone bridge over a broad moat, with courtyard ranges (now mostly gone) around it.
notes: A royal manor from 1305 (Bishop Bek), much used by Edward III, Richard II and Henry IV; the surviving great hall built for Edward IV c.1475-1480. Decayed after the Civil War and used as a barn; restored from 1911 and joined in 1933-36 to the Courtauld family's art deco house. Hall dimensions documented (100 x 36 ft); roof height estimated?

name: Lincoln's Inn Old Hall
style_hint: A small late-medieval hall of diapered red brick with stone dressings and a stepped or crow-gabled end, four-centred doorways, an oriel at the dais end and an open braced timber roof; low two-storey ranges of chambers alongside.
notes: Built 1489-1492; used as the Court of Chancery from 1737 to 1858 - the setting Dickens uses for Jarndyce v Jarndyce at the opening of Bleak House. Carefully restored/partly rebuilt 1924-28. Dimensions estimated?

name: Morton's Tower (Lambeth Palace gatehouse)
style_hint: A big five-storey twin-towered gatehouse in dark red diapered Tudor brick with stone dressings: two tall square turrets flanking a four-centred carriage arch with a pedestrian arch beside it, embattled parapets, small mullioned windows.
notes: Built 1495 for Cardinal John Morton; the principal public face of Lambeth Palace to the west. One of the earliest major brick buildings in London. Dimensions estimated from the listing?

name: Palace of Placentia, Greenwich (Tudor)
style_hint: Sprawling red-brick riverside palace: a long river front of ranges and bay windows facing north to the Thames, a five-storey donjon-like tower, two octagonal turreted towers overlooking a tiltyard on the east, a chapel, great hall, armoury and state apartments, with the park rising behind to the south.
notes: Rebuilt for Henry VII 1498-1504 under Robert Vertue. Birthplace of Henry VIII (1491, in the earlier house), Mary I (1516) and Elizabeth I (1533); Henry VIII's principal palace. Fell into decay under the Commonwealth (used as a biscuit factory and prisoner-of-war camp) and was demolished from 1660-1664 for Charles II's new King Charles Court, which in turn became Greenwich Hospital from 1694. Dimensions estimated from Wyngaerde's and Danckerts' views?

name: St John's Gate, Clerkenwell
style_hint: Tudor gatehouse: a four-centred stone archway with a lierne-vaulted carriageway flanked by two square projecting towers of three storeys, embattled parapets, mullioned and transomed windows, an oriel over the arch; Kentish ragstone with ashlar dressings.
notes: Built 1504 by Prior Thomas Docwra as the south gate of the priory precinct. Survives (much restored 1845-46 and 1873-74) as the Museum of the Order of St John; it was Edward Cave's printing house for The Gentleman's Magazine, where the young Samuel Johnson worked. Dimensions estimated from the listing description?

name: Woolwich Royal Dockyard
style_hint: Riverside naval yard with dry docks, covered slips, a mast house and the steam factory buildings of the 1830s-40s added along the frontage.
notes: Established 1512 to build the Henry Grace a Dieu; closed 1869. Extent given is the 19th-century yard, much larger than the Tudor one (?).

name: Deptford Royal Dockyard
style_hint: Royal naval yard on the Thames bend: two dry docks and a wet basin, timber-framed building slips under long pitched roofs, mast ponds, ropery and the brick Master Shipwright's house.
notes: Founded by Henry VIII in 1513; closed as a dockyard 1869 and became the Foreign Cattle Market, later Convoys Wharf. Long-axis bearing follows the river frontage (?).

name: Savoy Hospital
style_hint: Henry VII's hospital of St John the Baptist raised on the Savoy ruins: a large cruciform range of three long dormitory wings meeting at a central altar space, plus a chapel, master's lodging and service court, in brick and stone under tiled roofs.
notes: Founded by Henry VII's will, built 1512-1517, dissolved 1553, refounded, decayed through the 17th century and dissolved finally 1702; largely demolished 1816-1820 for the Waterloo Bridge approach. The Savoy Chapel (1512, rebuilt after 1864 fire) survives on the site. Dimensions estimated?

name: Westminster Abbey nave (completed)
style_hint: The western half of the church, deliberately built to match Henry III's 13th-century design 150 years later so that the whole reads as one: the same tall narrow bays, Purbeck shafts, triforium and 31 m vault, with a great west window and a temporary low west front until Hawksmoor's towers were added.
notes: Nave rebuilding restarted under Henry Yevele c.1376 and the fabric reached the west window by 1495; the vaulting and fitting-out ran on to about 1517 (dates for 'completion' vary between 1495 and 1532?). One of the most remarkable acts of deliberate stylistic continuity in European architecture.

name: Henry VII's Lady Chapel, Westminster Abbey
style_hint: The climax of English Perpendicular, added onto the abbey's east end: an aisled chapel with a polygonal apse of radiating chapels, walls dissolved almost entirely into glass between slender panelled buttresses topped by ogee-domed turrets, and inside the astonishing fan vault with hanging pendants that appear to float unsupported.
notes: Foundation stone 24 January 1503; main structure complete by 1509, fitting-out and the Torrigiano tomb continuing to about 1519. Called by Leland 'the wonder of the entire world'. Dimensions estimated?

name: Fulham Palace (Tudor courtyard)
style_hint: Country residence of the Bishops of London: a low two-storey quadrangle of warm red diapered Tudor brick around a small courtyard, with a gate-tower, a great hall on the east side, arched brick openings and tiled roofs; set inside what was once the longest domestic moat in England, with gardens to the Thames.
notes: The bishops held the manor from the 8th century; the surviving Tudor west quadrangle was built mainly under Bishops Fitzjames (1506-22) and Bonner, with earlier work from the 1480s. A Georgian east range was added by Bishop Terrick (1760s) and the chapel by Butterfield (1866). Ceased to be the bishop's residence 1973. Dimensions estimated from the courtyard plan?

name: Bridewell Palace
style_hint: Henry VIII's brick town palace on the Fleet: two brick courtyards, with the royal lodgings in three storeys around the inner court reached by a grand processional stair from the outer court; kitchens and a gatehouse on the north of the outer court, and a 240 ft gallery running south-west across the Fleet to link the palace to Blackfriars. Notably, the first royal palace built WITHOUT a great hall.
notes: Built 1515-1523; given by Edward VI in 1553 to the City, becoming Bridewell Hospital and then a house of correction - the prison ran 1556-1855 and gave its name to lock-ups generally. Demolished 1863-64. Dimensions estimated from the Agas map and excavation? The gallery length (240 ft) is documented.

name: Hampton Court Palace (Tudor)
style_hint: The greatest surviving Tudor palace: warm red brick with dark blue diaper patterning and stone dressings, a great embattled west gatehouse (Base Court), a second gate with Anne Boleyn's astronomical clock leading to Clock Court, Henry VIII's Great Hall with its huge hammerbeam roof and louvre, the Chapel Royal with a blue-and-gold vaulted ceiling, the Great Kitchens, and a famous forest of moulded and twisted brick chimney stacks over everything.
notes: Begun 1515 for Cardinal Wolsey, surrendered to Henry VIII in 1529 and hugely enlarged by him through the 1530s-40s (Great Hall 1532-35). About half the Tudor palace was demolished from 1689 for Wren's baroque ranges. Overall footprint is an approximation for the surviving Tudor half?

name: Palace of Whitehall
style_hint: Not one building but a sprawling accretion of over 1500 rooms across some 23 acres, straddling the public street: a dense band of brick and half-timbered ranges, courts, galleries, chapel and lodgings along the Thames on the east, and on the west a recreation zone with tiltyard (now Horse Guards Parade), cockpit, bowling green and four enclosed tennis courts, the two halves linked by the four-towered chequerwork Holbein Gate and the Kings Street Gate spanning the road.
notes: Originally York Place, the Archbishop of York's London house from c.1240; seized from Wolsey by Henry VIII in 1530 and expanded into the largest palace in Europe (larger than the Vatican or Versailles at the time). Destroyed by fire 4 January 1698 apart from the Banqueting House. Footprint here is the OVERALL EXTENT of the precinct (approx 430 x 230 m enclosing ~9.3 ha), not a single building - a modeller should treat it as a district. Centroid and extent are approximations?

name: Holbein Gate, Whitehall
style_hint: A four-storey gatehouse straddling the public road through the palace: four octagonal angle turrets with battlements and cupolas, a wide four-centred archway, and walls patterned all over in chequerwork of knapped flint and stone with terracotta roundel busts; upper rooms linking the two halves of the palace.
notes: Built 1531-32; the attribution to Holbein is traditional and almost certainly wrong. Demolished 1759 (some sources say 1769?) to widen Whitehall. Dimensions estimated from engravings?

name: St James's Palace
style_hint: Low, rambling red-brick Tudor palace of four courts: the famous north gatehouse of dark diapered brick with two tall octagonal turrets, battlements, a clock and a four-centred arch; two-storey ranges with mullioned windows and tall chimneys around Colour Court, Ambassadors' Court, Engine Court and Friary Court, plus the Chapel Royal.
notes: Built 1531-1536 for Henry VIII on the site of a leper hospital dedicated to St James. Became the principal royal residence after the 1698 Whitehall fire; still the senior royal palace (ambassadors are accredited to the Court of St James's). Much of the south and east was burnt in 1809 and rebuilt. Dimensions estimated from the plan?

name: Bermondsey House (Tudor mansion on the abbey site)
style_hint: Courtyard mansion converted by Sir Thomas Pope from the abbey's claustral ranges: two-storey brick and reused stone ranges around the former cloister garth, mullioned windows, gabled dormers, a gatehouse to the north.
notes: In place by 1541; progressively subdivided and decayed, effectively gone by the early 18th century (last fragments cleared c.1720-1830?). Dimensions estimated from the cloister footprint?

name: Charterhouse (Tudor mansion / Sutton's Hospital)
style_hint: Courtyard mansion made out of the priory's outer buildings: ranges of two storeys plus attics in dark red brick with stone dressings around Master's Court, a great hall with screens passage and a Great Chamber above, mullioned and transomed windows, stone-coped gables and tall clustered chimneys.
notes: Bought 1545 by Sir Edward North and converted; later the Duke of Norfolk's house; bought 1611 by Thomas Sutton, who endowed the almshouse and school that survive. Badly bombed 1941, restored 1950-59. Dimensions estimated?

name: Nonsuch Palace
style_hint: Henry VIII's fantasy showpiece, 'none such': two courts - a stone outer court with a gatehouse, and an inner court whose south front was timber-framed and covered in carved and gilded slate panels and moulded stucco duro reliefs of gods and emperors between vertical gilt slate strips, flanked by two tall five-storey octagonal towers with onion cupolas and gilt weathervanes.
notes: OUTSIDE central London - at Cheam, Surrey, about 20 km SW of the City, so probably outside the map frame. Begun 24 years to the day after Henry VIII's accession (1538), largely complete 1547. Granted by Charles II to Barbara Villiers, who demolished it about 1682-1690 to pay gambling debts. Excavated 1959 by Martin Biddle. Dimensions estimated from that excavation?

name: Dutch Church, Austin Friars (surviving friary nave)
style_hint: The truncated 14th-century friary nave alone, walled off at the east: six bays of tall arcades with aisles, big Decorated traceried windows, a plain gabled west front and a low pitched tiled roof; no tower after the 1633 spire fire.
notes: Granted by Edward VI in 1550 to Dutch Protestant refugees - the oldest Dutch-language Protestant congregation in the world. Gutted by a Luftwaffe incendiary raid on 15 October 1940 and cleared; replaced by Arthur Bailey's church of 1950-54. Nave dimensions estimated? - often quoted at about 150 x 80 ft.

name: Old Somerset House
style_hint: One of the first Renaissance buildings in England: a two-storey house of Bath and Caen stone round a quadrangle, its Strand front given a symmetrical triumphal-arch gateway rising to three storeys with superimposed classical orders, balustrades and pedimented windows; long gardens running south to a river terrace and watergate on the Thames.
notes: Built for Protector Somerset from 1547 (Wikipedia says work began c.1549 and Stow reported it still unfinished in 1598?) using stone robbed from demolished church buildings. Crown property after Somerset's fall in 1552; residence of Anne of Denmark, Henrietta Maria and Catherine of Braganza; hosted the Somerset House Conference of 1604. Demolished 1775-76 for Chambers's new Somerset House. Dimensions estimated from Kip's and Knyff's views?

name: Newgate (city gate)
style_hint: A tall gate of Kentish rag over the road to Holborn: a central carriage archway between two square embattled towers of three or four storeys with statues in niches, the upper chambers and adjoining buildings crammed with prison cells, and a barred window onto the street from which prisoners begged.
notes: A gate here from the Roman period; a prison in the gatehouse from 1188. Rebuilt with Dick Whittington's bequest 1423, again in 1555, burnt 1666 and rebuilt 1672. The gate itself was demolished 1777. Dimensions estimated from engravings?

name: Gray's Inn Hall
style_hint: An Elizabethan hall of about 70 x 35 ft with a fine carved oak screen (said to be made from the timbers of a Spanish Armada galleon), tall transomed windows, heraldic glass, a dais and an open timber roof; brick and stone, part of a courtyard of chambers.
notes: Built 1556-1560. The Comedy of Errors was performed here at the Gray's Inn revels on 28 December 1594. Gutted by bombing in 1941 and faithfully rebuilt 1951; the screen was saved. Dimensions of about 70 x 35 ft are the conventional figures? Roof height estimated.

name: Old St Paul's Cathedral (after the 1561 spire fire)
style_hint: The same enormous cross-shaped bulk but decapitated: a blunt square crossing tower of about 204 ft with a low temporary roof where the spire had been, badly decayed lead roofs, and (from 1642) Inigo Jones's brand-new classical portico jammed onto the medieval west front. The nave, 'Paul's Walk', was in use as a public thoroughfare and market.
notes: The spire was never rebuilt after 1561; the fabric decayed badly and was used as a market and stable during the Commonwealth. Gutted in the Great Fire 2-5 September 1666, when the roof lead ran molten down Ludgate Hill; demolition began 1668 and Wren's cathedral was begun 1675. Tower height 204 ft (62 m) from Robert Hooke's 1664 measurement.

name: Royal Exchange (first, Gresham's)
style_hint: Modelled on the Antwerp bourse and built by Flemish masons: a rectangular block round an open arcaded courtyard where merchants walked, with a covered loggia of round arches on Doric columns below and a gallery of about 100 small shops above; a bell tower over the south entrance carrying a giant gilt grasshopper (Gresham's crest), with more grasshoppers on the gables.
notes: Built 1566-1568 at Sir Thomas Gresham's own expense, opened and given its royal title by Elizabeth I on 23 January 1571. Destroyed in the Great Fire, 1666. Dimensions and tower height are estimates from engravings?

name: Middle Temple Hall
style_hint: The finest Elizabethan hall in London: a stone hall of about 101 x 41 ft with tall transomed windows, a splendid carved oak screen of 1574 at the west end, a raised dais with the 29 ft 'Bench Table' made from a single oak, and a magnificent double hammerbeam roof with pendants; heraldic glass and armour on the walls.
notes: Built 1562-1573 for the Middle Temple. Twelfth Night was performed here on Candlemas 1602 - one of the very few documented first-run Shakespeare performance venues still standing. Roof and screen damaged in 1940-41 and restored. Hall dimensions (101 x 41 ft) documented; roof height estimated?

name: Nonsuch House, London Bridge
style_hint: A four-storey Dutch Renaissance timber house built in prefabricated sections in the Netherlands and assembled on the bridge with wooden pegs and no nails: elaborately carved and gilded galleries overhanging the river on both sides, big mullioned windows, and four onion-domed corner cupolas with weathervanes; it straddled the roadway with an archway through it.
notes: Erected 1577-1579 on the site of the old drawbridge gate at the seventh and eighth piers from the Southwark end - the most famous building on Old London Bridge. Demolished 1757 with the rest of the bridge houses. All dimensions and the exact pier position are estimates?

name: Ludgate (city gate and prison)
style_hint: The westernmost city gate, on the slope down to the Fleet: a stone gate of one wide carriage arch with pedestrian arches beside it, flanked by square towers, statues of King Lud and his sons on the east face and Elizabeth I on the west, and rooms above and to the sides used as a debtors' prison with a grated begging window onto the street.
notes: A gate stood here from Roman/Saxon times; it housed a prison for freemen of the City from 1378. Rebuilt 1586, burnt in the Great Fire 1666, rebuilt 1668, and finally demolished in 1760 with the other city gates to ease traffic. Dimensions estimated from engravings?

name: The Rose theatre
style_hint: The smallest of the Bankside amphitheatres: a fourteen-sided polygon about 72 ft (22 m) across outside and 47 ft (14 m) across the yard, three galleries of timber on brick footings around a chalk-and-clinker yard sloping to the stage, a small tapered stage at the north, thatched gallery roofs.
notes: Built 1587 by Philip Henslowe and John Cholmley - the first purpose-built playhouse on Bankside. Enlarged in 1592 by moving the stage back about 6 ft 6 in, giving the distorted 'bulging tulip' plan found in excavation. Lease ended 1605 and it may have been pulled down as early as 1606. Excavated by the Museum of London in 1989 - the best-recorded Elizabethan playhouse; dimensions documented, heights estimated?

name: The Swan theatre
style_hint: Built by Francis Langley in Paris Garden, the westernmost Bankside house and said to be the largest and handsomest of its day: a round-reading polygon of flint concrete faced to imitate marble, three galleries seating about 3000, a large thrust stage on two painted columns supporting the heavens, tiring house with two doors, and a hut with a flag.
notes: Built c.1595. Famous as the subject of the ONLY surviving contemporary drawing of the interior of an Elizabethan playhouse - Johannes de Witt's sketch of c.1596, copied by Arend van Buchel. Fell out of theatrical use after 1621 and was derelict by the 1630s (dates for its end vary, 1632-1637?). Coordinates and all dimensions are estimates? - the site has never been securely located or excavated.

name: The Globe (first)
style_hint: A three-storey open-air amphitheatre, a 20-sided polygon about 100 ft across reading as a ring: timber frame on brick footings with lath-and-plaster infill, three tiers of roofed galleries facing an open yard, a rectangular thrust stage about 43 x 27 ft raised 5 ft, a canopied 'heavens' on two posts over the stage, a tiring-house behind, and a small hut with a flag turret above; thatched roof over the galleries.
notes: Built 1599 by the Lord Chamberlain's Men from the timbers of the dismantled Theatre in Shoreditch. Burnt down 29 June 1613 when a cannon fired during Henry VIII ignited the thatch. Only about 5% of the site was excavated (1989, under Anchor Terrace); the 100 ft diameter is an inference from that dig and from the Fortune contract - treat as an estimate? Orientation is nominal since the plan is polygonal - the stage faced roughly north-east.

name: The Globe (second)
style_hint: Rebuilt on the same foundations and reportedly finer than the first, but with a TILE roof instead of thatch after the fire; otherwise the same polygonal three-gallery amphitheatre with thrust stage, heavens and hut.
notes: Rebuilt June 1614 at a cost of about £1,400. Closed with all London theatres by the Puritan ordinance of 1642 and pulled down in 1644 or 1645 (sources differ?) for tenements.

name: The Hope theatre
style_hint: A dual-purpose house built by Henslowe on the site of the Bear Garden: a polygonal amphitheatre with three galleries and a tiled roof over them, but with a REMOVABLE trestle stage on props so the yard could be cleared for bear- and bull-baiting, and no stage posts - the heavens were cantilevered from the tiring house.
notes: Built 1613-14 by Philip Henslowe and Jacob Meade; Ben Jonson's Bartholomew Fair premiered here in 1614. Playing ceased about 1617 and it reverted to a baiting ring (the Bear Garden); pulled down 1656 when the Puritans killed the bears. Location and dimensions are estimates? - the site is roughly Bear Gardens, off Park Street.

name: Banqueting House, Whitehall
style_hint: England's first fully classical public building: a Portland stone box of seven bays, two superimposed orders of engaged Ionic below and Corinthian above on a rusticated basement, swagged frieze, balustraded parapet, flat roof. Inside is a single double-cube room 110 x 55 x 55 ft with a gallery, its ceiling filled by nine Rubens canvases of 1636.
notes: Built 1619-1622 by Inigo Jones for James I. Charles I was executed on a scaffold outside its first-floor windows on 30 January 1649. The only substantial part of Whitehall Palace to survive the 1698 fire. Refaced in Portland stone by Soane 1829. Interior dimensions (110 x 55 x 55 ft) documented; external height estimated?

name: St Paul's, Covent Garden
style_hint: Inigo Jones's 'handsomest barn in England': a plain rectangular box with a huge overhanging Tuscan portico of four columns facing the piazza, deep eaves, no tower
notes: Gutted by fire 1795, rebuilt to the same design by Thomas Hardwick. The portico doors are false; the altar is behind them.

name: Queen's House, Greenwich
style_hint: Inigo Jones, first true Palladian building in England: white rendered cube, rusticated ground floor, plain piano nobile, loggia of six Ionic columns on the south front, flat balustraded roof; originally an H-bridge over the Woolwich road
notes: Colonnades added 1807. Building is essentially a 34 m square?

name: Hyde Park
style_hint: Open green plane with the Serpentine lake cut across it in 1730; scattered tree masses, Rotten Row along the south edge; useful for the video as the largest void in the west of the frame
notes: Seized from Westminster Abbey 1536, opened to the public 1637. 142 ha; combined with Kensington Gardens 253 ha. Model as ground texture, not a building.

name: Inigo Jones's west portico, Old St Paul's
style_hint: A colossal Roman temple front pinned onto a Gothic cathedral: a deep Portland stone portico of giant fluted Corinthian columns (usually said to be ten across the front plus returns, some accounts say eight or twelve) about 45-56 ft tall, carrying a full entablature and a balustraded attic with statues of James I and Charles I; black marble steps below and huge Baroque stone volutes flanking the flanking stair turrets.
notes: Built 1633 to September 1642 by Inigo Jones as part of Charles I's restoration of the cathedral; reputedly the largest classical portico north of the Alps. Column count and height are inconsistent between sources (45 ft is usually quoted, but excavated column fragments imply about 56 ft)? Destroyed in the Great Fire; fragments survive in the Museum of London. Position offset ~90 m west of the cathedral centroid to sit at the west front.

name: Lambeth Palace Great Hall
style_hint: A deliberately archaic hall: tall stone walls with Gothic transomed windows and a big central louvre, carrying a wide hammerbeam roof of Restoration date but medieval in manner; now houses the Lambeth Palace Library.
notes: The medieval hall (13th century, remodelled 15th century) was demolished during the Commonwealth and rebuilt 1660-1663 by Archbishop Juxon in a retardataire Gothic style - Pepys called it 'a new old-fashioned hall'. Dimensions estimated?

name: Royal Exchange (second, Jarman's)
style_hint: Edward Jarman's post-Fire replacement: a heavier Baroque courtyard building with a two-storey arcaded ambulatory of coupled columns, statues of English monarchs in niches round the court, a grand pedimented and columned south entrance, and a tall square tower with a lead cupola and the grasshopper vane.
notes: Built 1667-69, opened 1669. The tower was replaced in 1821 by George Smith. Burnt down on the night of 10 January 1838 - the fire was reportedly visible from Windsor, 24 miles away. Dimensions and tower height are estimates?

name: St James's Square
style_hint: The first great aristocratic London square: four brick terraces of large town houses round a railed garden with a central equestrian statue of William III (1808); the model for the West End estate plan
notes: Laid out by the Earl of St Albans from 1665. Few original houses survive (No. 4 and No. 5 are late 17th-century in origin).

name: St Dunstan-in-the-East
style_hint: Medieval church repaired by Wren; Gothic-survival tower of 1695-1701 with a needle spire carried on four flying buttresses; body rebuilt 1817-21 in Perpendicular Gothic
notes: Body destroyed in the Blitz 1941; Wren tower and steeple survive over a public garden. Spire height approximate?

name: St Vedast-alias-Foster
style_hint: Small Wren church, plain body; concave-convex Baroque steeple of 1709-12 with obelisk spire, ~49 m
notes: Gutted 1940, restored 1962. Steeple height approximate?

name: St Bride's, Fleet Street
style_hint: Wren hall church, plain rectangular box with round-arched windows; famous telescoping octagonal wedding-cake steeple of four diminishing stages plus obelisk, 69 m (226 ft), tallest Wren steeple
notes: Steeple completed 1703. Gutted 1940, restored 1957.

name: Royal Observatory, Greenwich (Flamsteed House)
style_hint: Wren's small brick Flamsteed House on the hilltop: Octagon Room with tall windows, two corner turrets with ogee caps, red time-ball mast on the east turret (added 1833)
notes: Prime meridian at lon -0.001475. Later Victorian ranges to the east not modelled here.

name: St Magnus-the-Martyr
style_hint: Wren church at the old bridge foot; square west tower with octagonal lantern and lead cupola/spire 56 m (185 ft); open ground-floor arch once carried the footway onto Old London Bridge
notes: Tower/steeple completed 1706. Height 185 ft?

name: Monument to the Great Fire of London
style_hint: Fluted Doric column of Portland stone on a square plinth, viewing platform cage at 48 m, gilt flaming urn finial; exactly 61.57 m tall, its own height from the Pudding Lane bakery
notes: Wren and Hooke. Column diameter 4.6 m.

name: St Stephen Walbrook
style_hint: Wren's dome prototype for St Paul's: rectangular box roofed by a coffered dome on eight arches, lantern above; slender west tower with lead steeple added 1717, ~45 m
notes: Steeple height ~45 m?

name: St Mary-le-Bow (Wren)
style_hint: Wren's most admired City steeple: a plain rectangular galleried church of Portland stone on the Norman crypt, and at the west a square tower rising to a circular colonnaded temple of Ionic columns with flying buttresses shaped as scrolls, then a smaller square stage, then an obelisk spire and a gilt dragon weathervane, 224 ft in all.
notes: Rebuilt 1670-1680 by Christopher Wren, the steeple finished 1680 - it cost more than the church itself and became the model for church steeples across the English-speaking world. Gutted in the Blitz 11 May 1941 and restored by Laurence King 1956-64. Steeple 224 ft (72 m).

name: Christ Church Greyfriars (Wren)
style_hint: Wren galleried hall church on the nave footprint of the medieval Greyfriars church; square west tower with three-stage tiered steeple of diminishing colonnaded boxes, 47 m
notes: Gutted by incendiary bombs 29 Dec 1940; tower and walls survive as a rose garden ruin. Steeple completed 1704.

name: Christ Church Newgate Street (Wren)
style_hint: Wren city church built inside the footprint of the Greyfriars choir only: a rectangular five-bay galleried box with Corinthian columns, round-headed windows and a balustraded parapet, and a west tower carrying a three-stage diminishing square steeple with urns.
notes: Post-Fire rebuild 1677-1687, steeple completed 1704. Gutted by incendiaries on 29 December 1940; the tower and outer walls survive as a public garden. Steeple height about 153 ft (46 m)? Era label 'Stuart' used for the enum; the steeple is early Georgian.

name: Royal Hospital Chelsea
style_hint: Wren, brick with stone dressings: three long ranges around Figure Court opening south to the river; central octagonal vestibule with lantern and cupola, Doric portico, chapel and Great Hall flanking
notes: Overall spread including Light Horse and College Courts. Dimensions approximate from map inspection?

name: Hampton Court Palace (Wren east and south ranges)
style_hint: A restrained English baroque palace grafted onto the Tudor one and jarringly different from it: red brick with Portland stone dressings around Fountain Court, three storeys with a rusticated arcaded ground floor, tall round-headed windows to the state apartments, carved stone panels and a balustraded parapet with urns; the long east front faces the radiating avenues of the Home Park.
notes: Built 1689-1694 by Christopher Wren for William III and Mary II, who intended to demolish the whole Tudor palace; work stopped when Mary died in 1694, which is why both halves survive side by side. Dimensions estimated from the plan?

name: Buckingham House
style_hint: Modest red-brick three-storey house with pilasters and a balustraded parapet, flanking service wings joined by quadrant colonnades, facing east down the Mall
notes: Bought by George III 1761 as the Queen's House; encased and rebuilt by Nash from 1826.

name: Kensington Palace
style_hint: Low three-storey red-brick palace of linked courtyard blocks (Wren then Kent), no dominant tower; Clock Court with cupola, Orangery detached to the north
notes: Grew by accretion 1689-1728 from Nottingham House. Dimensions from map inspection?

name: St Paul's Cathedral (Wren)
style_hint: English Baroque cruciform cathedral, long nave, deep transepts, giant two-storey screen walls all round; crossing dome on drum with peristyle, golden ball and cross at 111.3 m; two west towers 65 m flanking a two-tier Corinthian portico
notes: Length 158 m, width across transepts 75 m; dome outer diameter 34 m. Replaced Old St Paul's burnt 1666. Roof/parapet height ~34 m approximate?

name: Marlborough House
style_hint: Wren the Younger, red brick with stone quoins, plain rectangular block of two main storeys with attic, low wings; a restrained town palace beside St James's Palace
notes: Raised a storey by Pennethorne 1861-63. Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Royal Hospital for Seamen / Old Royal Naval College, Greenwich
style_hint: Wren/Hawksmoor/Vanbrugh: four Baroque blocks in strict symmetry astride an axial vista from the river to the Queen's House; twin domes over the Painted Hall and Chapel, each on a colonnaded drum, ~55 m; long colonnades of paired Doric columns
notes: Built 1696-1751. Dome height approximate?

name: Hanover Square, Westminster
