style_hint: Early Georgian speculative square of plain brown-brick houses with a vista south down St George Street to the portico of St George's church.
notes: Laid out by the Earl of Scarbrough from 1713 and named for the new Hanoverian dynasty; St George's Hanover Square followed in 1725. Almost entirely rebuilt as commercial premises.

name: St Alfege, Greenwich
style_hint: Hawksmoor: giant east portico of four Doric columns under a broad pediment pierced by an arch; medieval tower recased with a spire by John James in 1730
notes: Roof burnt 1941, restored 1953. Tower height approximate?

name: Burlington House, Piccadilly
style_hint: Palladian mansion round a courtyard, refronted 1867-73 in Italianate stone with an added attic storey and a triumphal-arch gateway range across the Piccadilly frontage.
notes: Remodelled for the 3rd Earl of Burlington by Colen Campbell 1718-19; bought by the government in 1854 and raised a storey with new wings for the Royal Academy and the learned societies 1867-74. Birth date is the Palladian house.

name: Royal Arsenal, Woolwich
style_hint: Ordnance manufactory behind a long river wall: the Royal Brass Foundry, the arcaded Grand Store and the Dial Square laboratory ranges, plain brick with stone dressings and low pitched roofs.
notes: Warren estate bought 1671, formally the Royal Arsenal from 1805; Royal Brass Foundry 1717, Grand Store 1806-13. Munitions work ended 1967 and the survivors are now housing. Extent is the historic core, not the 5 km wartime site (?).

name: Guy's Hospital (Georgian courts)
style_hint: Plain brown-brick quadrangle of three storeys with stone dressings, an arcaded ground floor and a small pedimented chapel; a second court added 1738-80.
notes: Founded by Thomas Guy in 1721, the first court finished 1725; the courts survive in front of the later Hunt's House and Guy's Tower. Dimensions approximate (?).

name: Admiralty (Ripley Building), Whitehall
style_hint: Three-storey brick U-plan block round an open court with a heavy Ionic portico of four columns, screened from Whitehall by Robert Adam's stone screen wall with paired Doric columns.
notes: Thomas Ripley 1723-26; Adam's screen added 1759-61. Coordinates are those of Admiralty House next door (?) - the Ripley Building lies a few metres north.

name: St Martin-in-the-Fields
style_hint: James Gibbs, the model copied worldwide: giant hexastyle Corinthian portico to the west, and a tall stone steeple of diminishing stages rising through the roof ridge behind it, 58 m (192 ft)
notes: Steeple 192 ft.

name: St Anne's Limehouse
style_hint: Hawksmoor: tall west tower with a circular stair projection and an octagonal lantern with clock (the highest church clock in London), semicircular porch, heavy Portland stone
notes: Tower height approximate?

name: St Mary Woolnoth
style_hint: Hawksmoor's smallest and densest: a near-cubic rusticated stone block, north wall banded with heavy rustication, twin square turrets side by side on a single broad west tower
notes: Bank station booking hall built into the crypt 1897-1900. Tower height approximate?

name: Chiswick House
style_hint: Miniature Palladian villa after the Villa Capra: a cube of Portland-faced brick with a hexastyle Corinthian portico reached by twin stairs, and a low octagonal dome over the central saloon.
notes: Built by Lord Burlington with William Kent 1726-29 beside the older Jacobean house (demolished 1788). Dome height above ground approximate (?).

name: Christ Church, Spitalfields
style_hint: Hawksmoor at his most massive: deep Tuscan portico of four columns under a giant broken arch, square tower rising through it into a tall broach spire, ~69 m; heavy blank side walls with Venetian windows
notes: Spire height approximate?

name: Marble Hill House, Twickenham
style_hint: A perfect small white Palladian villa in a riverside lawn: rusticated basement, plain stuccoed cube, pedimented centre, hipped roof - the model for countless Georgian houses
notes: Represents the Thames-side Palladian villas (with Chiswick House 1729, Ham House 1610, Syon).

name: Fulham Bridge (old Putney Bridge)
style_hint: Timber piled trestle bridge on driven oak piles with a plank deck.
notes: Timber toll bridge authorised by the Fulham and Putney Bridge Act 1725, built by the carpenter Thomas Phillips to designs by Sir Jacob Ackworth, Surveyor of the Navy; opened 29 November 1729. For many years the only bridge between London Bridge and Kingston. About 786 ft (240 m) long on 26 narrow timber piers, with tollbooths at each end; two spans replaced by a single iron span in 1870-72 to ease navigation. Bought by the Metropolitan Board of Works in 1879, tolls ended 1880, demolished after the new bridge opened in 1886. Stood roughly 30 m downstream (east) of the present bridge, aligned on Putney and Fulham parish churches; coordinates derived from that offset (?). kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category available. Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: St George in the East
style_hint: Hawksmoor: blocky stone box, west tower with an octagonal lantern crowned by a stone drum, plus four odd 'pepper-pot' stair turrets at the corners
notes: Gutted by bombing 1941; a smaller modern church built inside the shell 1964. Tower height approximate?

name: St George's, Bloomsbury
style_hint: Hawksmoor: six-column Corinthian portico to the south, and a stepped pyramid steeple modelled on the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus with a statue of George I on top, ~46 m
notes: Steeple height approximate?

name: Grosvenor Square
style_hint: Very large Mayfair square, originally ranges of brown-brick houses with stone dressings round a railed oval garden; rebuilt piecemeal in stone and brick 1900-60.
notes: Laid out for Sir Richard Grosvenor from 1721 and essentially complete by 1731. Almost no original houses survive, so the birth date refers to the first build-out.

name: Bank of England (Sampson building)
style_hint: George Sampson's first purpose-built Bank: a modest Palladian street front on Threadneedle Street with a courtyard behind
notes: Progressively absorbed into Taylor's and then Soane's Bank; not demolished at one moment. Death year nominal?

name: Berkeley Square
style_hint: Long narrow Mayfair square of brick terraces round a garden of plane trees planted in 1789; no. 44 (William Kent, 1744) has the finest staircase in London.
notes: Laid out from 1738 on the garden of Berkeley House. The east side was largely rebuilt as offices in the 20th century.

name: Foundling Hospital, Bloomsbury
style_hint: Two long plain brick wings of three storeys flanking an open forecourt, joined by a colonnade, with a pedimented chapel on the axis between them.
notes: Theodore Jacobsen's building of 1742-52 for Thomas Coram's hospital; vacated 1926 and demolished 1928, the grounds becoming Coram's Fields. Dimensions estimated from engravings (?).

name: Westminster Abbey west towers (Hawksmoor)
style_hint: A pair of matching Portland stone towers of Gothick-classical hybrid design flanking the west window: square shafts rising in receding panelled stages, tall two-light belfry openings, big clock faces, and open crocketed pinnacles at the four corners of each, about 225 ft high.
notes: Designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor, begun under him from 1722 and completed after his death in 1745 by John James. Height about 225 ft (69 m)? - not confirmed on the Wikipedia article. Era label 'Stuart' used only to satisfy the enum - these are Georgian.

name: Westminster Bridge (Labelye)
style_hint: Masonry arch bridge with rusticated voussoirs, cutwater piers and a balustraded parapet.
notes: Designed by the Swiss engineer Charles Labelye, built 1739-50 and opened 18 November 1750; the second bridge in central London after London Bridge, famously the subject of Wordsworth's sonnet of 1802. Fifteen semicircular stone arches on caisson-founded piers, about 1,223 ft (373 m) long with a roadway around 30 ft wide inside a total width of about 44 ft (?). Subsided badly and was expensive to maintain; replaced in stages and finally removed in 1861 (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Mansion House
style_hint: George Dance the Elder, Palladian: rusticated basement, six-column Corinthian portico with a sculpted pediment reached by a broad flight of steps; originally had two tall attic 'Mayor's Nest' roof structures over the Egyptian Hall (removed 1794 and 1842)
notes: Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Hampton Court Bridge (first)
style_hint: Timber piled trestle bridge on driven oak piles with a plank deck.
notes: Built 1752-53 by Samuel Stevens and Benjamin Ludgator, opened 13 December 1753. Seven timber arches in an elaborate Chinoiserie style reflecting the fashionable Willow pattern; a toll bridge. Structurally weak and short-lived. kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category. Coordinates assumed the same as the present bridge (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Horse Guards
style_hint: William Kent / John Vardy, Palladian: long low three-part front of pale stone with end pavilions, a central clock tower with an ogee lead cupola, and an arched carriage passage from Whitehall through to the parade ground
notes: Replaced an earlier 1660s guard house. Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Kew Bridge (first, Tunstall)
style_hint: Timber piled trestle bridge on driven oak piles with a plank deck.
notes: Opened 1 June 1759, designed by John Barnard and built by Robert Tunstall as a toll bridge replacing the Kew ferry. Two stone arches at each end with seven timber arches between; over 3,000 people crossed on the opening day. Lasted only 30 years because of the cost of maintaining the timber spans. Stood a short distance downstream of the later bridges; coordinates approximate (?). kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category. Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Great Pagoda, Kew Gardens
style_hint: William Chambers' chinoiserie folly: ten octagonal storeys of diminishing width in grey brick, each with a projecting roof and (restored 2018) 80 gilded dragons, ~50 m
notes: Height 163 ft / 49.7 m.

name: Lansdowne House, Berkeley Square
style_hint: Adam mansion of Portland stone set back behind a forecourt on the south side of Berkeley Square, with a low pedimented centre and flanking wings.
notes: Begun by Robert Adam for Lord Bute in 1762 and finished for Lord Shelburne; the front rooms and forecourt were destroyed in 1935 when Fitzmaurice Place was driven through, the remainder becoming the Lansdowne Club. The death date marks the 1935 truncation, not total loss (?).

name: Spencer House, St James's
style_hint: Palladian town palace whose Green Park front carries a giant pedimented order of Doric columns crowned by statues - the finest surviving 18th-century private house front in London.
notes: John Vardy and James 'Athenian' Stuart, 1756-66, for the 1st Earl Spencer; stripped during the war and restored 1985-90.

name: Blackfriars Bridge (Mylne)
style_hint: Masonry arch bridge with rusticated voussoirs, cutwater piers and a balustraded parapet.
notes: Designed by Robert Mylne in an Italianate style, built 1760-69 and opened as a toll bridge in 1769; originally named William Pitt Bridge. Nine semi-elliptical arches of Portland stone, 995 ft (303 m) long. Tolls abolished 1785. Weakened by scour after the removal of Old London Bridge changed the tidal regime; some sources say dismantling began in 1860 and others give demolition in 1864 (?). Width approximate (?). Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: St Bartholomew's Hospital (Gibbs quadrangle)
style_hint: Four detached Palladian blocks of Bath stone forming an open square around a courtyard with a fountain: three storeys over a rusticated ground floor, pedimented centres, sash windows, hipped slate roofs; the North Wing contains the Great Hall and Hogarth's painted staircase.
notes: Designed by James Gibbs, built in four separate blocks 1730-1769 (North Wing 1732, then West, South and East). The Henry VIII Gate to Smithfield dates from 1702. Era label 'Stuart' used only to fit the enum - this is Georgian. Quadrangle dimensions estimated?

name: Syon House, Isleworth
style_hint: Plain castellated square block of Bath stone round a central courtyard with square corner turrets, hiding Robert Adam's most sumptuous neoclassical interiors; Adam screen and lion facing the river.
notes: Tudor shell of 1547 on the site of Syon Abbey, remodelled inside by Adam for the 1st Duke of Northumberland 1762-69; the great conservatory added 1826. Birth date is the Adam remodelling (?) - the fabric is Tudor.

name: Old Battersea Bridge
style_hint: Timber piled trestle bridge on driven oak piles with a plank deck.
notes: Timber toll bridge on the site of the Chelsea-Battersea ferry, opened to pedestrians in November 1771 and to vehicles in 1772. 734 ft (224 m) long, 24 ft (7.3 m) wide, with 19 narrow spans (widest 32 ft) that boats struck constantly. Painted repeatedly by Whistler and Turner. Two spans were replaced by iron girders in 1873 to ease navigation. Closed and demolished 1885. kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category available - this was an 18th century timber trestle, not a Roman bridge. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: The Adelphi (Adam terrace)
style_hint: Neoclassical river terrace of eleven houses raised on a honeycomb of brick vaults and arches above the Thames foreshore, the front pilastered and picked out with Adam honeysuckle ornament.
notes: Built by the four Adam brothers 1768-72 on the site of Durham House; the Royal Terrace was demolished in 1936 for the present Adelphi office block, though the vaults survive under the streets. The river front faced south until the Victoria Embankment (1870) pushed the water away.

name: Strawberry Hill House, Twickenham
style_hint: White-rendered Gothick fantasy of asymmetrical bays, battlements, quatrefoil windows and a round tower with a conical cap - the building that launched the Gothic Revival.
notes: Built for Horace Walpole in stages 1749-76, extended by Lady Waldegrave 1860-62 and restored 2010-12. Facade bearing to the Thames lawn approximate (?).

name: Richmond Bridge
style_hint: Masonry arch bridge with rusticated voussoirs, cutwater piers and a balustraded parapet.
notes: The oldest surviving Thames bridge in London. Built 1774-77 by James Paine and Kenton Couse to replace a ferry, opened to traffic 12 January 1777 and completed December 1777; a toll bridge until 1859. 300 ft (91 m) long, five elliptical Portland stone arches of varying height with a humpbacked profile and a tall 60 ft central span for shipping. Widened by about 11 ft and slightly flattened in 1937-40. Grade I listed. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Apsley House (No. 1 London)
style_hint: Robert Adam red-brick villa, refaced in Bath stone by Wyatt 1828-30 with a four-column Corinthian portico; the first house past the Hyde Park turnpike
notes: Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Hampton Court Bridge (second)
style_hint: Timber piled trestle bridge on driven oak piles with a plank deck.
notes: Replacement timber bridge of eleven arches, sturdier and plainer than its Chinoiserie predecessor; opened 1778. By the 1840s it was condemned as 'crazy, hog-backed, inconvenient and obstructive of the navigation'. kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category. Coordinates assumed the same as the present bridge (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Newgate Prison (George Dance the Younger)
style_hint: The most famous exercise in 'architecture terrible' in Britain: a long, almost windowless wall of heavily vermiculated rusticated Portland stone with festooned niches and a giant blind arcade, three storeys but reading as one forbidding cliff, with a keeper's house in the centre and courtyards for felons, debtors and the condemned hidden behind; the public gallows stood against the Old Bailey front from 1783.
notes: Built 1770-1778 by George Dance the Younger, gutted in the Gordon Riots of 1780 and rebuilt by 1783. Public executions moved here from Tyburn in 1783 and continued in front of it until 1868. Closed 1902 and demolished 1904 for the Central Criminal Court (Old Bailey, 1907). Era label 'Stuart' only to satisfy the enum - this is Georgian. Dimensions estimated?

name: Kenwood House, Hampstead
style_hint: Long white stuccoed villa on the ridge above the Heath: Adam's Ionic portico on the north entrance front and a pedimented library wing balancing the orangery on the south garden front.
notes: Remodelled by Robert Adam for the 1st Earl of Mansfield 1764-79; wings added by George Saunders 1793-96. Given to the nation with the Iveagh Bequest in 1927.

name: Osterley Park House
style_hint: Elizabethan brick courtyard house recased by Adam, entered across an open portico of twelve Ionic columns raised on a broad flight of steps between four corner turrets.
notes: Adam's transformation for the Child banking family 1761-80 of a house of about 1576. Sits just inside the western edge of the modelled frame.

name: Portland Place
style_hint: Exceptionally wide straight street of stuccoed and brick terraces by the Adam brothers, forming the northern leg of Nash's route from Carlton House to Regent's Park.
notes: Built by James and Robert Adam 1773-c.1790 and absorbed into Nash's Regent Street scheme 1811-25. Length about 420 m, roadway about 38 m wide. Many houses have been replaced (Broadcasting House 1932, RIBA 1934).

name: Bedford Square
style_hint: The most complete Georgian square in London: four uniform brick terraces, each treated as a single palace front with a stuccoed pedimented centre, around an oval private garden
notes: Represents the Georgian squares generally (Grosvenor 1720s, Berkeley, Fitzroy, Russell 1800).

name: Dover House, Whitehall
style_hint: Palladian mansion given a circular domed entrance hall and an Ionic screen to Whitehall by Henry Holland; Portland stone, three storeys.
notes: Original house by James Paine 1755-58; Holland's Whitehall screen and rotunda 1787. Now the Scotland Office. Dimensions estimated (?).

name: Carlton House
style_hint: Neoclassical prince's palace: Corinthian hexastyle portico to Pall Mall behind a low Ionic screen colonnade; long garden front of two storeys over a rusticated basement facing St James's Park.
notes: Henry Holland's remodelling for the Prince of Wales 1783-89, further altered to 1813; demolished 1826-27 when George IV moved to Buckingham Palace. Its Corinthian columns were reused on the portico of the National Gallery. Footprint and height estimated from Horwood/Britton plans (?); the facade bearing to Pall Mall is firm, depth (?).

name: Kew Bridge (Paine)
style_hint: Masonry arch bridge with rusticated voussoirs, cutwater piers and a balustraded parapet.
notes: All-stone bridge designed by James Paine, opened 22 September 1789 by George III. About 1,000 ft (305 m) long including approaches with a 56 ft roadway; seven arches. Tolls abolished in 1873 when the Metropolitan Board of Works bought it. Too narrow and steep for growing traffic; closed and demolished around 1898-1902 for the present bridge - death year 1898 approximate (?). Width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Fitzroy Square
style_hint: Small square whose east and south sides are palace-fronted Portland stone terraces by Robert Adam with pilastered centrepieces; the north and west sides were finished in brick after 1827.
notes: Adam's east side 1792-98, south side completed 1798; the later sides 1827-35. Severely bombed in the 1940s and restored.

name: Somerset House (Chambers)
style_hint: Sir William Chambers, huge Palladian government quadrangle; Strand block of nine bays, vast courtyard, and a rusticated river terrace on arches that originally stood in the Thames before the Embankment of 1870
notes: Replaced Old Somerset House. King's College east wing 1829-35, west wing 1856. Dimensions from map inspection?

name: West India Docks, Isle of Dogs
style_hint: Two parallel rectangular ship basins cut across the neck of the Isle of Dogs, lined with five- and six-storey yellow-brick warehouses and enclosed by a 6 m boundary wall with a Doric guardhouse.
notes: Import Dock opened 1802, Export Dock 1806; the first enclosed wet docks, with a legal monopoly on West India produce. Closed 1980 - the basins survive as the water of Canary Wharf and No. 1 Warehouse remains as the Museum of London Docklands. Death date is closure; most warehouses went between the 1930s and 1980s (?).

name: London Docks, Wapping
style_hint: Western and Eastern basins behind a high brick wall, ringed by tall stock-brick warehouses over vaulted wine cellars, with the wide iron-and-timber Tobacco Dock shed.
notes: Daniel Alexander and John Rennie, opened 1805; closed 1969 and the basins largely filled during the 1970s-80s for News International's plant and housing. Tobacco Dock (1811) survives.

name: East India Docks, Blackwall
style_hint: Import and Export basins with a short entrance basin to the Thames, lined with low sheds rather than warehouses because East India cargoes were carted up to the City warehouses.
notes: Opened 1806 by the East India Dock Company; heavily bombed 1940, closed 1967 and largely filled - Brunswick Wharf power station and later housing took the site.

name: Surrey Commercial Docks, Rotherhithe
style_hint: A sprawl of nine timber ponds and basins covering most of the Rotherhithe peninsula, edged by open stacking grounds and low sheds rather than tall warehouses.
notes: Grew from the Howland Great Wet Dock of 1696; the Commercial Dock Company system dates from 1807 and handled the Baltic softwood trade. Closed 1970 and nearly all filled for Surrey Quays; only Greenland Dock and South Dock remain as water.

name: Royal Mint, Tower Hill (Smirke building)
style_hint: Sober Greek Revival ashlar block, a seven-bay centre with pedimented Doric portico and flanking pavilions, set behind railings on a walled coining yard.
notes: Designed by James Johnson and completed under Robert Smirke 1809-12; coining moved to Llantrisant in 1968 and the site is now Royal Mint Court. Footprint covers the main frontage block only (?).

name: Theatre Royal, Drury Lane (Wyatt)
style_hint: Fourth theatre on the site: a brick and stucco block with a giant Ionic portico and, from 1831, a cast-iron colonnade along the flank; the largest playhouse in London.
notes: Benjamin Dean Wyatt, 1811-12, after the 1809 fire destroyed Henry Holland's theatre; portico 1820, Russell Street colonnade 1831. Facade bearing to Catherine Street approximate (?).

name: Sir John Soane's Museum, Lincoln's Inn Fields
style_hint: Narrow three-bay town house with a projecting Portland stone loggia of three storeys, incised Greek-key ornament and top-lit domed interiors packed with antiquities.
notes: No. 13 rebuilt by Soane 1812-13 (nos. 12 and 14 are 1792 and 1824); made a public museum by Act of Parliament 1833. On the north side of the square, so the front faces south.

name: Lord's Cricket Ground
style_hint: Oval turf ground ringed by low stands, dominated by Verity's Victorian brick-and-stucco Pavilion with its two turrets, and since 1987 by the tented Mound Stand and the pod-like Media Centre.
notes: Thomas Lord's third ground, opened on the present St John's Wood site in 1814; the Pavilion is 1889-90 by Thomas Verity, the Mound Stand 1987 (Hopkins) and the Media Centre 1999. Modelled mass is the modern ground (?).

name: Bethlem Royal Hospital, St George's Fields
style_hint: James Lewis: a very long low symmetrical brick range of 175 m with a central Ionic portico; Sydney Smirke added the copper dome over the chapel in 1846
notes: Third Bethlem; predecessors at Bishopsgate (1247) and Moorfields (Hooke, 1676-1815). Hospital moved to Beckenham 1930; the wings were demolished and the centre block became the Imperial War Museum in 1936.

name: Vauxhall Bridge (Regent Bridge)
style_hint: Cast- or wrought-iron arch ribs springing from stone piers, with iron spandrel tracery.
notes: The first iron bridge over the Thames, designed by James Walker after an abandoned stone design by John Rennie; opened 4 June 1816 as Regent's Bridge, later Vauxhall Bridge. Nine cast iron arches on stone piers, about 809 ft (247 m) long. Toll bridge until bought by the Metropolitan Board of Works in 1879. Piers undermined by tidal scour; demolition began in 1898 with a temporary timber bridge alongside from August 1898 until 1906. Width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Custom House, Lower Thames Street
style_hint: David Laing, long low Neoclassical river front of 150 m with a recessed Ionic colonnade over the Long Room; centre collapsed 1825 and was rebuilt by Robert Smirke
notes: Fifth Custom House on the site; predecessors of 1275, 1559, Wren's 1671 (burnt 1714) and Ripley's 1718 (burnt 1814).

name: Waterloo Bridge (Rennie)
style_hint: Masonry arch bridge with rusticated voussoirs, cutwater piers and a balustraded parapet.
notes: Designed by John Rennie the Elder, opened 18 June 1817 on the second anniversary of the battle; originally to be called Strand Bridge. Nine semi-elliptical arches of 120 ft span separated by paired Doric columns, in Cornish granite. 1,240 ft (378 m) between abutments, 2,456 ft (748.6 m) including approaches - length_m here is the river structure. Toll bridge until nationalised in 1878. Piers settled badly from 1923; closed and demolished from 1936, the demolition being publicly controversial. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Southwark Bridge (Rennie)
style_hint: Cast- or wrought-iron arch ribs springing from stone piers, with iron spandrel tracery.
notes: Designed by John Rennie the Elder, built 1814-19 and opened 1819 as a toll bridge. Three cast iron arches on granite piers, the 240 ft (73.2 m) centre span being the longest cast iron span ever built. Cost GBP 700,000; fifty men died in construction. Known as the 'Iron Bridge' and appears in Dickens's Little Dorrit. Closed 1913 and demolished to make way for the present bridge; demolition ran into the First World War (?). Length and width approximate (?). Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: HM Prison Brixton
style_hint: The oldest London prison still in use; began as the Surrey House of Correction with a treadwheel, much rebuilt 1850s as a women's convict prison
notes: Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Regent's Canal Dock (Limehouse Basin)
style_hint: Rectangular ship basin linking the Regent's Canal and the Limehouse Cut to the Thames through a lock, ringed by coal wharves and hydraulic cranes.
notes: Opened with the Regent's Canal in 1820 and enlarged 1852-69 for seagoing colliers; commercial traffic ended 1969 and it is now a marina. Dimensions approximate (?).

name: Millbank Penitentiary
style_hint: Vast brick star-plan penitentiary: a central hexagonal chapel and governor's block ringed by six three-storey pentagons of cells, the whole inside an octagonal boundary wall and a moat on the Thames bank.
notes: Begun 1812 to a plan derived from Bentham's panopticon, occupied from 1816 and complete 1821; closed 1890, demolished 1892-1903, the site taken by the Tate Gallery and the Royal Army Medical College. Covered about 16 acres (6.5 ha) - the 350 m square is the outer wall envelope (?).

name: Park Crescent, Regent's Park
style_hint: Nash's semicircular stucco crescent with a continuous paired-Ionic colonnade at ground level, forming the hinge between Portland Place and Regent's Park
notes: Rebuilt behind facades after WWII damage.

name: All Souls, Langham Place
style_hint: Nash's hinge in the Regent Street plan: a circular Ionic peristyle porch carrying a needle-sharp conical stone spire, so the church reads the same from every angle as the street bends
notes: Spire height approximate?

name: Regent Street (Nash)
style_hint: Nash's stuccoed processional street from Carlton House to Regent's Park; the Quadrant originally had a continuous Doric colonnade over the pavement (removed 1848); uniform four-storey painted stucco terraces
notes: Almost entirely rebuilt in Portland stone 1895-1927 (Norman Shaw, Reginald Blomfield). Represent as a linear street object.

name: Cumberland Terrace, Regent's Park
style_hint: Nash/Decimus Burton: the grandest Regent's Park terrace, a 240 m painted stucco palace front of three blocks linked by triumphal arches, giant Ionic portico with a sculptured pediment in the centre
notes: Length approximate?

name: Hammersmith Bridge (Tierney Clark)
style_hint: Suspension bridge: chains or cables slung between masonry or iron towers over a light deck.
notes: The first suspension bridge over the Thames, designed by William Tierney Clark and opened 6 October 1827 at a cost of GBP 80,000. 822 ft 8 in (250.75 m) total with 688 ft 8 in (209.91 m) of clear waterway and a 688 ft (210 m) main span; wrought iron bars, stone towers, timber roadway with granite surfacing. Carriageway 20 ft (6.1 m) plus two 5 ft footways. Overloaded by 11,000-12,000 spectators at the 1870 Boat Race, prompting replacement; closed 1884 and replaced by a temporary bridge during construction of the present one. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Belgrave Square
style_hint: Grandest of the Cubitt squares: four stuccoed palace-fronted terraces of four storeys with giant Corinthian pilasters plus four detached corner mansions, round a large private garden.
notes: Laid out by Thomas Cubitt for the Grosvenor estate from 1826 and mostly finished 1828-40; architect George Basevi.

name: Kingston Bridge
style_hint: Masonry arch bridge with rusticated voussoirs, cutwater piers and a balustraded parapet.
notes: Classical Portland stone bridge by Edward Lapidge, county surveyor of Surrey; foundation stone laid by the Earl of Liverpool 7 November 1825, opened by the Duchess of Clarence 17 July 1828. Five elliptical arches, originally 382 ft (116.43 m) long and 27 ft (8.2 m) wide with a 60 ft centre span. Widened on the downstream side 1912-14 to 55 ft, and again in 2000 to 79 ft (24.08 m) for cycle and bus lanes - width given is the modern width. Carries about 50,000 vehicles a day on the A308. Grade II* listed 1951. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: St Katharine Docks
style_hint: Two irregular basins round a central island, the warehouses standing directly on the quay edge on cast-iron Doric columns so cargo swung straight from ship to store; six storeys of brick.
notes: Thomas Telford (engineer) with Philip Hardwick (warehouses), opened 25 October 1828 after 1,250 houses and the medieval hospital of St Katharine were cleared. Badly bombed 1940; closed 1968 and redeveloped as a marina from 1973.

name: Athenaeum Club, Pall Mall
style_hint: Stuccoed Greek Revival clubhouse with a Doric porch under a gilded statue of Athena and a full-length Parthenon frieze in Wedgwood blue and white below the cornice.
notes: Decimus Burton, 1827-30; attic storey added 1899. Faces east onto Waterloo Place - facade bearing approximate (?).

name: Covent Garden Market building
style_hint: Charles Fowler's granite market: three long parallel ranges with Tuscan colonnades and pavilions, glass roofs added 1875-89; Floral Hall 1860, Jubilee Market 1904
notes: Fruit and vegetable market moved to Nine Elms 1974; building reopened as shops 1980. Inigo Jones's piazza dates from 1630s.

name: Wellington Arch (Constitution Arch)
style_hint: Decimus Burton, single-opening Corinthian triumphal arch; carried a huge equestrian Wellington 1846-1883, since 1912 crowned by Adrian Jones's bronze quadriga of Peace descending on the chariot of War
notes: Moved about 30 m to its present position on the Hyde Park Corner island in 1882-83.

name: New London Bridge (Rennie)
style_hint: Masonry arch bridge with rusticated voussoirs, cutwater piers and a balustraded parapet.
notes: Designed by John Rennie the Elder, built by his son John Rennie the Younger; opened 1 August 1831. Five semi-elliptical arches of Haytor granite, built 100 ft (30 m) upstream (west) of the medieval bridge. Widened 1902-04 to about 20 m, which contributed to its settling. Sold 18 April 1968 to Robert P. McCulloch, dismantled 1968-1971 and the facing stones re-erected at Lake Havasu City, Arizona. Death year given as 1967 (closure to traffic / start of replacement); physical removal completed 1971 (?). Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Bank of England (Soane's Bank)
style_hint: Soane's masterpiece: a 1.4 ha island site enclosed by a blank windowless curtain wall of Portland stone with a Corinthian order and the Tivoli Corner rotunda; inside, a low landscape of top-lit domed banking halls, no upper storeys
notes: Site ~3.5 acres. All but the curtain wall demolished 1925-39 - 'the greatest architectural crime of the 20th century in the City'.

name: Kensal Green Cemetery
style_hint: The first of the Magnificent Seven: a long strip of parkland beside the Grand Union Canal with a Greek Revival Doric entrance arch and Anglican chapel with a colonnade over catacombs
notes: 72 acres. Extent approximate?

name: Marble Arch
style_hint: Nash's white Carrara marble triumphal arch on the Arch of Constantine model: three openings, Corinthian columns, attic storey; originally the state entrance to Buckingham Palace
notes: Stood before Buckingham Palace (51.50139, -0.14194) 1833-1851, moved to the NE corner of Hyde Park 1851, marooned on a traffic island 1960-61.

name: Regent's Park
style_hint: Nash's circular park ringed by white stucco terraces, with an inner circle, a boating lake and the Zoo at the north end; the terraces are the built edge worth modelling, the interior is green
notes: Opened to the public 1835. London Zoo opened 1828.

name: London Bridge station
style_hint: London's first railway terminus, carried into Southwark on a long brick viaduct of 878 arches; a confusing double station of through and terminal platforms, wholly rebuilt 2013-18 with a single vast street-level concourse under the tracks
notes: Opened 1836 (first section Feb 1836). Successive rebuilds 1849, 1864, 1978, 2013-18 not given separate entries.

name: Euston Arch (Doric propylaeum)
style_hint: Bridgnorth-gritstone propylaeum: four baseless Greek Doric columns 8.5 m high in antis under a plain entablature, flanked by two lodges, forming the ceremonial gateway to the railway.
notes: Philip Hardwick, 1837; 70 ft (21.3 m) high, the largest Doric portico ever built. Demolished 1961-62 despite a national campaign; some stones were recovered from the Prescott Channel in 1994.

name: Euston station (original)
style_hint: Two shallow wrought-iron train sheds behind a screen of offices and, from 1849, Hardwick's Great Hall - a coffered Roman basilica 38 m by 18 m with a double sweeping staircase to the shareholders' room.
notes: London terminus of the London and Birmingham Railway, opened 20 July 1837; Great Hall 1849. Everything except the war memorial and the two lodges was demolished 1961-62.

name: Royal College of Surgeons of England
style_hint: Greek Revival stone front of six giant Ionic columns carrying a plain entablature above a rusticated basement.
notes: George Dance the Younger and James Lewis 1813, rebuilt behind the portico by Charles Barry 1835-37; bombed 1941 and rebuilt with the portico retained. On the south side of Lincoln's Inn Fields, facing north.

name: National Gallery
style_hint: William Wilkins: long thin Neoclassical front the full width of Trafalgar Square, a Corinthian portico of columns reused from Carlton House, a small central dome and two little turrets often mocked as pepperpots
notes: Sainsbury Wing added 1991 to the west. Dome height approximate?

name: Highgate Cemetery
style_hint: Terraced Victorian garden cemetery on a hillside; Egyptian Avenue of lotus columns leading into the sunken Circle of Lebanon, a ring of mausolea around an ancient cedar, and Gothic chapels at the gate
notes: One of the Magnificent Seven. Extent approximate (both halves) ?

name: HM Prison Pentonville
style_hint: The 'model prison' whose radial plan was copied worldwide: five (originally four) long cell wings fanning from a central hall and inspection point, inside a rectangular walled yard with a castellated gatehouse
notes: Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Nelson's Column
style_hint: Fluted Corinthian granite column on a square pedestal, 5.5 m sandstone statue of Nelson on top, total 51.6 m; four bronze lions by Landseer added round the base 1867
notes: Height 169 ft 3 in / 51.6 m as re-measured 2006 (long quoted as 56 m).

name: Royal Exchange (third, Tite's)
style_hint: Trapezoidal Portland stone block wedged between Threadneedle Street and Cornhill: a giant octastyle Corinthian portico with a sculpted pediment facing west onto the junction, ranges of arched windows along the flanks, an internal courtyard (roofed with glass in 1883-84), and a campanile of 177 ft at the east end carrying the original 1571 grasshopper vane.
notes: Designed by Sir William Tite, opened by Queen Victoria 28 October 1844, trading began 1 January 1845. Campanile 177 ft (54 m) above street level - documented. Era label 'Stuart' used only to satisfy the enum; this is early Victorian.

name: Trafalgar Square
style_hint: Terraced public square stepping down from the National Gallery terrace to a broad paved level with two fountains and Nelson's Column, held by a balustraded retaining wall with four plinths.
notes: Laid out by John Nash from 1826 on the old Royal Mews and completed to Charles Barry's design 1840-45; fountains rebuilt by Lutyens 1937-39, north terrace steps 2003. Height figure is the terrace drop, not a building.

name: Hungerford Suspension Footbridge (Brunel)
style_hint: Suspension bridge: chains or cables slung between masonry or iron towers over a light deck.
notes: Designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel to serve Hungerford Market, opened 1 May 1845. Central span 676 ft (206 m) with two side spans; Italianate brick towers. Bought in 1859 by the Charing Cross Railway Company and demolished in 1860-62 to make way for the railway bridge; the wrought iron chains were re-used on Brunel's Clifton Suspension Bridge in Bristol, and the brick piers were partly reused. Total length and width approximate (?). Death year 1860 marks the start of removal (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Lincoln's Inn Great Hall and Library
style_hint: Big Victorian Tudor-revival group in red brick with black diapering and stone dressings: a tall hall with an open hammerbeam roof and a huge G. F. Watts fresco at the dais end, joined at right angles to the library range, with an octagonal turret and tall clustered chimneys.
notes: Built 1843-45 by Philip Hardwick and opened by Queen Victoria in 1845. Era label 'Stuart' used only to satisfy the enum - this is Victorian. Dimensions estimated?

name: The Oval, Kennington
style_hint: Broad oval ground on a former market garden, its skyline defined for a century by the two Kennington gasholders just outside the Vauxhall End.
notes: Leased by Surrey CCC in 1845; hosted the first Test match in England in 1880 and the first FA Cup final in 1872. Pavilion 1898 by Thomas Muirhead; stands rebuilt 2005 and 2013.

name: Palm House, Kew Gardens
style_hint: Great curved glasshouse like an upturned hull: wrought-iron ribs and 16,000 panes of green-tinted glass over a central barrel with lower wings, the boiler smoke carried off by a detached Italianate campanile.
notes: Decimus Burton with the ironfounder Richard Turner, 1844-48; 110 m long, central span 30 m, height 19 m. Restored 1955-57 and 1984-88.

name: Richmond Railway Bridge
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Opened 1848, designed by Joseph Locke and J. E. Errington; among the first railway crossings of the Thames. Three spans totalling 91.5 m. The original cast iron arches were replaced in situ with steel by John Wykeham Jacomb-Hood in 1906-08, reusing the piers and abutments and reproducing the 1848 appearance; deck and girders renewed again in 1984. Treated here as one continuous structure rather than split into 1848 and 1908 entries (?). Carries National Rail between Richmond and St Margarets. Grade II listed 2008. Width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Waterloo station (original)
style_hint: A notoriously incoherent sprawl grown by accretion, platforms added piecemeal on a brick viaduct with no unified roof or numbering
notes: Progressively replaced 1900-1922, so death date is nominal.

name: Barnes Railway Bridge (Locke, original)
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Designed by Joseph Locke for the Richmond and Windsor Railway, built from 1846 by Fox Henderson & Co and opened 22 August 1849. Two pairs of cast iron arch spans of 36.57 m with a rise of 3.66 m, six ribs each 915 mm deep, on brick piers faced with Bramley Fall stone, carrying a timber deck. Superseded in 1895 but the arches physically survive alongside the newer bridge on the upstream side, disused. Coordinates offset slightly upstream of the 1895 bridge (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Coal Exchange, Lower Thames Street
style_hint: One of the first substantial cast-iron buildings: a circular glass-domed rotunda 60 ft across, ringed by three tiers of iron galleries painted with coal-trade motifs, behind a stone front with a corner tower.
notes: J. B. Bunning, 1847-49, opened by Prince Albert 30 October 1849. Demolished in 1962 to widen Lower Thames Street despite a Victorian Society campaign - one of the losses that hardened the conservation movement. Rotunda 60 ft (18 m) internal diameter; tower height (?).

name: Buckingham Palace
style_hint: Quadrangle palace, Nash's Bath-stone garden front to the west, Blore's east front of 1847-50 closing the courtyard, refaced in Portland stone by Aston Webb 1913 with a flat classical facade of 1913 and the Victoria Memorial on axis; 108 m east front
notes: East front 108 m long; whole block ~120 m N-S x ~108 m E-W. Marble Arch stood before the east front 1827-1851.

name: The Crystal Palace, Hyde Park (Great Exhibition)
style_hint: Prefabricated cast-iron and plate-glass shed of stepped tiers, a flat-roofed nave of three levels crossed by a great barrel-vaulted transept high enough to enclose the park's elm trees; 293,000 panes of glass on a 24 ft module.
notes: Joseph Paxton's building for the Great Exhibition, erected in 39 weeks and open 1 May - 15 Oct 1851; 1,851 ft (564 m) long, interior height 128 ft (39 m), 990,000 sq ft of floor. Dismantled 1852 and re-erected at Sydenham. Position on the south side of Hyde Park parallel to Rotten Row is approximate (?) - no plaque survives.

name: HM Prison Wandsworth
style_hint: The largest prison in western Europe: two radial clusters of cell wings (originally separate male and female prisons) inside a long perimeter wall, Italianate brick gatehouse
notes: Dimensions from map inspection?

name: British Museum (Smirke)
style_hint: Robert Smirke, Greek Revival: a hollow square of ranges round a courtyard, with a 44-column Ionic colonnade and eight-column portico across the whole south front
notes: Round Reading Room added in the courtyard 1857 (dome 42.6 m diameter, 32 m high).

name: HM Prison Holloway
style_hint: Originally a castellated Gothic 'City House of Correction' modelled on Warwick Castle, with a great turreted gatehouse and stone griffins; wholly rebuilt 1971-85 as low brick blocks
notes: Women-only from 1903. Closed 2016, demolished from 2021. Original Victorian building demolished from 1971.

name: King's Cross station
style_hint: Lewis Cubitt: brutally plain yellow-brick front of two huge semicircular arches expressing the two 32.6 m train sheds behind, with an Italianate clock turret between them; western concourse shell added 2012
notes: Sheds 32.6 m span each, ~240 m long. Clock tower height approximate?

name: Kennington (Oval) gasholders
style_hint: Two large telescopic gasholders in tiered lattice guide frames rising directly behind the Vauxhall End - the most recognisable backdrop in English cricket.
notes: Built for the Phoenix Gas Company from the 1850s (holder No. 1 is 1853); the surviving frame is Grade II listed. Coordinates, diameter and height approximate (?).

name: Crystal Palace, Sydenham
style_hint: Enlarged and wholly vaulted version of the Hyde Park building on the crest of Sydenham Hill: a barrel-vaulted nave with three transepts, standing above vast Italianate terraces and fountains, flanked by two Brunel water towers.
notes: Re-erected and greatly enlarged 1852-54, opened by Queen Victoria 10 June 1854; central transept 168 ft (51 m) high, the two Brunel water towers 282 ft (86 m). North transept burnt 1866; the whole palace destroyed by fire on the night of 30 November 1936. The towers were demolished in 1941. Long axis runs north-south along the ridge with the show front east over the terraces.

name: Fenchurch Street station
style_hint: The City's smallest terminus, raised on a viaduct: a symmetrical yellow-brick front with a big lunette window under a curved gable, and a modest arched shed behind
notes: First station 1841; present frontage 1854. Office block built over it 1987 keeping the facade.

name: Paddington station
style_hint: Brunel with Digby Wyatt: three parallel wrought-iron and glass arched spans (21 m, 31 m, 21 m) crossed by two glazed transepts, decorative Moorish tracery in the end screens; a fourth span added 1916
notes: Spans 68/102/70 ft. Great Western Royal Hotel of 1854 fronts Praed Street.

name: Royal Victoria Dock
style_hint: First of the Royal Docks and the first designed for steamships and served by rail: a mile-long rectangular basin with finger jetties on the north quay and hydraulic warehouses.
notes: Opened 1855; nearly a mile (1.6 km) long. Closed to commercial traffic 1981. The water survives, with ExCeL along the north quay.

name: British Museum Round Reading Room
style_hint: Cast-iron and concrete drum filling the museum's quadrangle, carrying a shallow papier-mache-lined dome 42.6 m across, ringed by radiating desks and three tiers of bookstacks.
notes: Sydney Smirke, 1854-57; dome 140 ft (42.6 m) in diameter and 106 ft (32.3 m) high, then the second-widest dome in the world. Closed to readers 1997 and enclosed by the Great Court roof in 2000.

name: Battersea Park
style_hint: Victorian riverside park laid out on drained marshland, boating lake, riverside promenade; Festival Pleasure Gardens 1951, Peace Pagoda 1985 on the embankment
notes: 83 ha. Model as ground texture.

name: Chelsea Bridge (Victoria Bridge)
style_hint: Suspension bridge: chains or cables slung between masonry or iron towers over a light deck.
notes: Designed by Thomas Page, built 1851-58 and opened 3 April 1858 as Victoria Bridge; renamed Chelsea Bridge as its structural weakness became known. 703 ft (214 m) long, 47 ft (14 m) wide with a 32 ft roadway and 7.5 ft footpaths; central span 333 ft (101 m). Wrought iron deck with ornate cast iron towers. Demolished 1934-37; death year given as 1935 as the mid-point of demolition (?). Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Royal Opera House, Covent Garden
style_hint: Classical stone front with a hexastyle Corinthian portico carrying Flaxman's reliefs salvaged from the earlier theatre, behind it a tall fly-tower and the iron-framed Floral Hall.
notes: Edward Middleton Barry's third theatre on the site, opened 15 May 1858 after the 1856 fire; Floral Hall 1860, wholly rebuilt behind the facade 1990-99. Portico faces east onto Bow Street.

name: Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben)
style_hint: Square Gothic Revival clock tower, brick core clad in Anston stone, 12 m square; four 7 m clock dials at 55 m, then a cast-iron spire with pinnacles and the Ayrton Light, total 96.3 m
notes: Great Bell (Big Ben) hung 1858, clock started 31 May 1859. Renamed Elizabeth Tower 2012; refurbished 2017-2022.

name: Grosvenor Bridge (Victoria Railway Bridge)
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: The first railway bridge across the Thames in central London, built 1859-60 by the Victoria Station and Pimlico Railway for GBP 84,000 to carry two tracks into Victoria; engineer Sir John Fowler. Widened by four tracks on the east side 1865-66 (engineer Sir Charles Fox, GBP 245,000), and again in 1907 with a further track on the west side for the LBSCR. In 1963-67 the whole superstructure was renewed by Freeman Fox & Partners, leaving only the cores of the original piers, and a tenth track added. Now nine tracks, Network Rail. Structurally a series of iron/steel arches rather than lattice trusses; kind set to rail_lattice as the nearest category (?). Width given is the modern width; the 1860 bridge was about 12 m wide (?). Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Victoria Tower
style_hint: Massive square Gothic keep-like tower, 22.9 m square and 98.5 m tall, the tallest building in the world when finished; Royal Entrance arch at the base, iron-framed record floors above, flagstaff and cast-iron crown
notes: Height 98.5 m.

name: Metropolitan Tabernacle, Elephant and Castle
style_hint: Grecian preaching-house with a giant hexastyle Corinthian portico, built to hold 5,000 hearers for Charles Spurgeon.
notes: William Willmer Pocock, opened 18 March 1861; gutted by fire 1898 and by bombing 1941, each time rebuilt behind the surviving portico.

name: Lambeth Bridge (Barlow)
style_hint: Suspension bridge: chains or cables slung between masonry or iron towers over a light deck.
notes: Designed by Peter W. Barlow, opened 10 November 1862 as a toll bridge on the site of the ancient Lambeth horse ferry. 828 ft (252.4 m) long. Widely disliked and structurally poor; badly corroded, it was closed to vehicles by 1910 and used only by pedestrians before demolition around 1929 to make way for the present bridge. Width and deck height approximate (?). Death year 1929 approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Royal Agricultural Hall, Islington
style_hint: Single iron-arched roof of 125 ft clear span over a brick-walled hall, with a gabled and arcaded entrance front to Upper Street.
notes: Frederick Peck, opened 1862; used for the Smithfield Show, Cruft's and the World's Fair. Derelict from 1971, restored as the Business Design Centre 1986.

name: London Victoria station
style_hint: Two separate stations side by side behind one frontage: the Brighton side (1860) and the Chatham side (1862), each with its own iron shed; Edwardian Portland-stone Grosvenor Hotel front rebuilt 1908
notes: Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Westminster Bridge
style_hint: Cast- or wrought-iron arch ribs springing from stone piers, with iron spandrel tracery.
notes: Seven cast iron arches by engineer Thomas Page with Gothic detailing by Charles Barry to harmonise with the new Palace of Westminster; opened 24 May 1862. 820 ft (250 m) long, 85 ft (26 m) wide. Painted green to match the benches of the House of Commons. Grade II* listed 1981. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Battersea Railway Bridge (Cremorne Bridge)
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Opened to traffic 2 March 1863 for the West London Extension Railway; engineer William Baker. Originally the Cremorne Bridge (after Cremorne Gardens), also Battersea New Bridge, and officially Chelsea River Bridge to Network Rail. Five wrought iron arches flanked by brick approach viaducts: 230 m over the river, 387.1 m overall; longest span 42.5 m. Carries the West London Line (London Overground Mildmay line). The most complete survivor of the six 1860s Thames railway bridges; Grade II* listed 2008. Structurally arched rather than lattice; kind set to rail_lattice as the nearest rail category (?). Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Kingston Railway Bridge
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Opened 1863 for the London and South Western Railway; the original cast iron structure was replaced by the present steel bridge in 1907 by John Wykeham Jacomb-Hood, treated here as one continuous structure (?). Five spans, three over the river and two over land, with two piers in the water; deck about 22 ft 4 in (6.81 m) above the water. Carries the Kingston Loop line between Kingston and Hampton Wick stations. Length and width approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Temperate House, Kew Gardens
style_hint: The largest surviving Victorian glasshouse: a long rectangular iron-and-glass hall with stone-clad plinth and end pavilions, twice the floor area of the Palm House.
notes: Decimus Burton, central block 1860-63, the octagons and wings completed 1898; restored 2013-18. Coordinates approximate (?).

name: Blackfriars Railway Bridge (first, St Paul's)
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Designed by Joseph Cubitt for the London, Chatham and Dover Railway, opened 1864; five wrought iron arch spans on cast iron columns, with heavy abutments bearing the LCDR insignia. Became too weak for modern trains and its deck was removed in 1985, leaving the red-painted cast iron piers standing in the river and the Grade II listed southern abutment with its LCDR crest. Immediately upstream (west) of the 1886 bridge; coordinates derived from that offset (?). Length and width approximate (?). rebuilt_as points to the 1886 bridge as functional successor, but the two coexisted 1886-1985. Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Charing Cross station and Charing Cross Hotel
style_hint: Single 50 m crescent-truss arched shed over six platforms reached straight off Hungerford Bridge; E. M. Barry's French Renaissance hotel across the front, with a replica Eleanor Cross of 1865 in the forecourt
notes: Original arched roof partly collapsed 1905 killing six; replaced by a flat ridge-and-furrow roof. Embankment Place office deck built over the tracks 1990.

name: Hungerford Bridge (Charing Cross Railway Bridge)
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Wrought iron / steel lattice truss railway bridge designed by Sir John Hawkshaw, opened 1864 to carry the South Eastern Main Line into Charing Cross station. Replaced Brunel's suspension footbridge and reused its piers. Originally carried narrow pedestrian walkways on both sides, later only the downstream one, until the Golden Jubilee Bridges replaced them. A three-year refurbishment of the truss metalwork began in January 2025. Length and width approximate (?). Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Queen Eleanor Memorial Cross, Charing Cross station
style_hint: A taller, freer Victorian Gothic emulation: an octagonal stepped base rising through three heavily crocketed and gabled stages with eight statues of Queen Eleanor by Thomas Earp, topped by a slender pinnacled spirelet and cross; Portland stone, Mansfield stone and grey granite.
notes: Erected 1865 by E. M. Barry for the South Eastern Railway in the forecourt of Charing Cross station, about 200 m north-east of the original cross's site. 70 ft (21 m) high. Era label 'Stuart' used only to satisfy the enum - this is Victorian.

name: Crossness Pumping Station
style_hint: Romanesque yellow-brick engine house with round-arched windows, containing four rotative beam engines inside a riot of painted ornamental cast ironwork on a central octagon.
notes: Charles Driver for Bazalgette, 1859-65, at the end of the Southern Outfall Sewer; opened by the Prince of Wales 4 April 1865, decommissioned 1956. Now a preserved museum. Well east of the main scene - importance kept low.

name: Hampton Court Bridge (third)
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Built 1864-65 with wrought iron lattice girders resting on four cast iron columns. Highly profitable as a toll bridge, taking over GBP 3,000 a year, but widely condemned as 'one of the ugliest bridges in England'. Tolls ended 1876 when Surrey and Middlesex county councils bought it. Demolished for the present bridge in 1933. kind set to rail_lattice to capture the lattice-girder form although it was a road bridge. Coordinates assumed the same as the present bridge (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Cannon Street Railway Bridge (Alexandra Bridge)
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Built 1863-66 for the South Eastern Railway, engineers John Hawkshaw and John Wolfe Barry, opened 1866. Originally five wrought iron spans carrying five tracks on cast iron cylinder piers. Widened to ten tracks and about 120 ft (37 m); the rebuilt bridge reopened 13 February 1892. Further strengthened 1913 with six new 443 ft girders, and the deck was renewed in the 1980s. Some sources date the bridge 1866 and others 1883 or 1892 for the widened structure (?). Width quoted is post-widening; original width about 24 m (?). Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Cannon Street station
style_hint: Hawkshaw's great 57 m single-span arched shed running straight off the river bridge, flanked by two tall Italianate brick towers with lead-domed cupolas at the river end - the station's signature silhouette
notes: Roof glass removed in WWII, ironwork scrapped 1958; the two river-side towers and side walls survive. Office block over the platforms 1960s and again 2007.

name: King's Cross gasholders (Pancras gasworks)
style_hint: Telescopic water-sealed gasholders inside ornamented cast-iron guide frames of clustered Doric columns and lattice girders, standing in a triplet beside the Regent's Canal.
notes: Guide frames of the Imperial Gas Light and Coke Company's Pancras works, 1860-83 (holder No. 8 dated 1883). Dismantled 2001 for the Channel Tunnel Rail Link and re-erected 2013-18 as Gasholder Park and Gasholders London flats. Height and diameter approximate (?).

name: Abbey Mills Pumping Station
style_hint: Cruciform Byzantine-Venetian engine house of polychrome brick with a lantern and cupola over the crossing, once flanked by two Moorish octagonal chimneys - Bazalgette's 'cathedral of sewage'.
notes: Charles Driver for Joseph Bazalgette, 1865-68; eight beam engines, two on each arm. The two 64 m ornamental chimneys were demolished in 1941 as bombing landmarks - set spire to null after 1941. Facade bearing (?).

name: Foreign, India, Colonial and Home Offices, Whitehall
style_hint: Gilbert Scott's Italianate palazzo block (forced on him instead of his preferred Gothic), four departments round two courtyards, the glass-roofed Durbar Court of the India Office in the middle; grand Whitehall and St James's Park fronts with statues and a corner tower
notes: The 'Battle of the Styles' building. Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Smithfield Market (London Central Markets)
style_hint: Horace Jones: a long Italianate market hall of red brick, Portland stone and cast iron, 192 m by 74 m, cut in two by the Grand Avenue arcade, with octagonal corner turrets with lead domes and elaborate iron gates; railway sidings in the vaults below
notes: Poultry Market added 1875 (rebuilt 1963 with a 68 m concrete dome). Turret height approximate?

name: St Pancras station and Midland Grand Hotel
style_hint: Barlow's single-span iron train shed, 73.2 m clear span and 30.5 m to the apex, the widest in the world when built, standing on an undercroft of beer-barrel columns; in front, Gilbert Scott's polychrome Gothic Midland Grand Hotel with a clock tower of 82 m and a west tower of 76 m
notes: Hotel opened 1873. Clock tower 82 m (269 ft).

name: Blackfriars Bridge
style_hint: Cast- or wrought-iron arch ribs springing from stone piers, with iron spandrel tracery.
notes: Five wrought iron arches designed by Joseph Cubitt, opened by Queen Victoria on 6 November 1869. Originally 70 ft (21 m) wide; widened between 1907 and 1910 to 105 ft (32 m) to take trams, making it one of the widest bridges in London. Carries the A201. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Columbia Market, Bethnal Green
style_hint: Extraordinary Gothic market hall in the manner of a cathedral chapter house - a groin-vaulted hall of granite and stone with a fretted clock tower, gargoyles and a quadrangle of Gothic shops.
notes: Built for Baroness Angela Burdett-Coutts by H. A. Darbishire, opened 28 April 1869; a commercial failure, closed 1889 and demolished about 1958-60 for the Dorset Estate. Only gates and railings survive. Dimensions estimated from photographs (?).

name: Holborn Viaduct
style_hint: A 430 m raised road bridging the Fleet valley; the showpiece is a 32 m cast-iron span over Farringdon Street with winged lions, bronze statues of Commerce, Agriculture, Science and Fine Art, and four ornate Renaissance step-buildings at the corners
notes: Two of the four corner buildings destroyed in WWII and rebuilt 2001. Bridge span 107 ft.

name: Kew Railway Bridge
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Opened 1 January 1869 between Kew and Strand-on-the-Green, Chiswick; engineer W. R. Galbraith, builders Brassey & Ogilvie, for the London and South Western Railway. 575 ft (175 m) long, five spans of about 35 m, wrought iron lattice girders on cast iron piers. Carries two electrified tracks used by the London Overground Mildmay line and the London Underground District line. Grade II listed 1983. Width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Palace of Westminster (Barry and Pugin)
style_hint: Charles Barry's symmetrical Perpendicular Gothic river front 265 m long, encrusted by Pugin; deliberately asymmetric skyline of Victoria Tower at the south end, the octagonal Central Lobby spire at 91 m in the middle, and the Clock Tower at the north; Westminster Hall of 1097 embedded on the west side
notes: Occupied from 1852; officially complete 1870. Central Tower spire 91 m.

name: Tower Subway
style_hint: Cast-iron tube of 7 ft internal diameter bored through the London clay with Greathead's shield, with small round brick entrance shafts and drum-shaped kiosks at each end.
notes: Dug 1869 and opened August 1870 with a cable-hauled carriage, then converted to a foot tunnel; closed to the public in 1898 after Tower Bridge opened and now carries water mains. Sub-surface - render as the two entrance kiosks only, or omit. Length 1,340 ft (410 m).

name: Royal Albert Hall
style_hint: Red brick and terracotta elliptical amphitheatre 83 m by 72 m, ringed by a 244 m mosaic frieze, roofed by a shallow glazed wrought-iron dome; fibreglass acoustic 'mushrooms' hung inside 1969
notes: Height to top of dome ~41 m?

name: St Thomas' Hospital, Lambeth
style_hint: Seven detached Italianate pavilion blocks of red brick and stone in a line along the Albert Embankment, connected by low corridors - the built demonstration of Florence Nightingale's ward theory.
notes: Henry Currey, 1868-71, after the hospital was displaced from Southwark by the railway; opened by Queen Victoria 21 June 1871. Three of the seven blocks were destroyed by bombing and replaced by the 1966-76 tower and podium. Faces west across the river to the Palace of Westminster.

name: Albert Memorial
style_hint: Gilbert Scott's giant Gothic ciborium: a gilded seated Albert under a jewelled and enamelled canopy on a stepped platform, spire and cross to 54.2 m, with four marble Continents groups at the outer corners
notes: Statue installed 1875. Height 176 ft.

name: Albert Bridge
style_hint: Suspension bridge: chains or cables slung between masonry or iron towers over a light deck.
notes: Opened 23 August 1873, designed by Rowland Mason Ordish on his patented Ordish-Lefeuvre cable-stayed system with 32 inclined stays. 710 ft (220 m) long, 41 ft (12 m) wide, original central span 384 ft 9 in (117.27 m). Strengthened by Sir Joseph Bazalgette in 1884-87 with conventional suspension chains, and again in 1973 when the GLC added two concrete piers mid-river turning the centre into a simple beam - so it is now a hybrid of three bridge types. Nicknamed 'the Trembling Lady'; troops are ordered to break step. Grade II* listed. Closed in February 2026 for repairs to cracked cast iron (?). Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Wandsworth Bridge (Tolme)
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Wrought iron lattice truss road bridge on five spans by Julian Tolme, opened 26 September 1873 at a cost of GBP 40,000. Only 30 ft (9.1 m) wide, a commercial failure as a toll bridge, freed from tolls in 1880. Weight-restricted from 1935 and demolished in 1937. kind set to rail_lattice to capture the lattice-truss form although it was a road bridge. Length and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Alexandra Palace
style_hint: Enormous brick and iron people's palace on a north London ridge: a central Great Hall under a semicircular roof with a rose window, flanked by long ranges and low corner towers, terraced above the park to the south.
notes: Opened 1873 by John Johnson and Alfred Meeson, burnt out sixteen days later and reopened 1 May 1875; the Great Hall was again gutted by fire in 1980 and restored. Heights approximate (?).

name: Liverpool Street station
style_hint: Great Eastern terminus sunk below street level; four-span iron roof on slender clustered columns with Gothic spandrels, a cathedral-like western trainshed; Great Eastern Hotel 1884 in front
notes: Opened 1874, completed 1875. Heavily rebuilt 1985-91 keeping the western shed.

name: Queen Anne's Mansions, Westminster
style_hint: Gaunt unadorned cliff of dark brick rising fourteen storeys straight off the pavement without setbacks - by far the tallest residential block in Britain and widely loathed.
notes: Built speculatively by Henry Alers Hankey as his own architect from 1873, first stage 1875, raised to fourteen storeys (about 46 m) by 1890. The outrage it caused led to the height limits of the London Building Act 1894. Demolished 1971-73 for the Home Office building. Height approximate (?).

name: Billingsgate Fish Market (Lower Thames Street)
style_hint: Horace Jones's yellow-brick and Portland stone river front with arcaded openings, French pavilion roofs and two dolphin weathervanes; a wide top-lit trading floor behind
notes: Fish market moved to Docklands (Poplar) in 1982; building converted to offices 1988. Death year = end of market use, building survives.

name: Stamford Bridge
style_hint: Originally an open athletics bowl with a single pavilion, rebuilt from 1972 and again in the 1990s as an enclosed four-stand football ground with cantilever roofs; capacity about 40,000.
notes: Opened as the London Athletic Club ground in 1877; Chelsea FC was founded to play there in 1905 with an Archibald Leitch grandstand. The present stands date from 1974 (East), 1994-2001 (the rest), so the modelled mass suits the late 20th century rather than 1877 (?).

name: Union Chapel, Islington
style_hint: Powerful red-brick Gothic octagon with a soaring corner tower and spire, its galleried auditorium arranged in the round for preaching.
notes: James Cubitt, 1876-77, the tower and spire finished 1889 at about 52 m (?).

name: Old Kent Road gasholder No. 13
style_hint: Single enormous telescopic gasholder in a two-tier lattice guide frame, for many years the largest gasholder in the world and a fixed landmark of south-east London.
notes: Built 1879-81 for the South Metropolitan Gas Company at the Old Kent Road works; roughly 300 ft (91 m) in diameter. Coordinates, diameter and height are approximate (?) - the works has no dedicated article. Dismantled in the 2010s.

name: Royal Albert Dock
style_hint: Immense straight cutting nearly two miles long, lit by electricity from the start and lined with single-storey transit sheds rather than warehouses.
notes: Opened 24 June 1880 as an eastward extension of the Royal Victoria; closed 1981. London City Airport's runway was laid between it and the King George V Dock in 1987.

name: Leadenhall Market
style_hint: Horace Jones: cruciform glazed arcade of wrought iron and glass painted cream, maroon and green, over cobbled lanes, with a small octagonal crossing dome; built on the site of the Roman forum
notes: Market on the site since the 14th century.

name: Natural History Museum
style_hint: Alfred Waterhouse's 'cathedral to nature': a 205 m Romanesque front entirely faced in buff and blue-grey terracotta moulded with animals, a great round-arched central portal and two symmetrical towers of about 58 m
notes: Front 675 ft. Tower height approximate?

name: Royal Courts of Justice
style_hint: G. E. Street's last work, a picturesque Victorian Gothic pile of Portland stone with over 1,000 rooms, a 24 m vaulted Great Hall, a clock tower and a taller square Records tower, spiky roofline of gables and turrets on the Strand
notes: Tower heights approximate?

name: Blackfriars Railway Bridge
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Wrought iron bridge built by Lucas and Aird, engineers John Wolfe Barry and Henry Marc Brunel, opened 1886 with St Paul's station (renamed Blackfriars 1937). Five spans: two middle spans of 185 ft, shore spans 183 ft, secondary spans 175 ft. Clear width 81 ft (24.7 m) between parapets, widening to 123 ft at the northernmost span. Rebuilt and extended 2009-2012 to carry the Thameslink Blackfriars station across the whole river, with a solar-panel roof. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Olympia Grand Hall, West Kensington
style_hint: Vast glazed iron barrel roof of 170 ft clear span over an unobstructed hall, behind a brick and terracotta front; the widest unsupported span in England when built.
notes: Henry E. Coe, opened 27 December 1886 as the National Agricultural Hall; National Hall added 1923 and Empire Hall 1929. Roof span 170 ft (52 m); footprint and ridge height approximate (?).

name: Putney Bridge
style_hint: Masonry arch bridge with rusticated voussoirs, cutwater piers and a balustraded parapet.
notes: Five-arch stone and granite bridge designed by Sir Joseph Bazalgette, opened 29 May 1886 by the Prince and Princess of Wales. 700 ft (210 m) long and originally 43 ft (13 m) wide; widened in 1933 to three carriageways, so the modern width is about 22 m (?). Marks the start of the Oxford and Cambridge Boat Race course. Grade II listed; maintained by Wandsworth Council. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Hammersmith Bridge
style_hint: Suspension bridge: chains or cables slung between masonry or iron towers over a light deck.
notes: Suspension bridge by Sir Joseph Bazalgette using the original 1827 pier foundations, built by Dixon, Appleby & Thorne and opened 11 June 1887 at a cost of GBP 82,117. 700 ft (210 m) long, 43 ft (13 m) wide, main span 400 ft (120 m), in steel and wrought and cast iron with ornate painted ironwork. Grade II* listed. Closed to motor traffic in April 2019 after cracks were found in the cast iron pedestals, and closed entirely August 2020 - February 2021; still restricted. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Whitehall Court
style_hint: Extravagant French chateau silhouette of turrets, dormers, chimneystacks and steep roofs in red brick and stone, presenting a fantastic skyline to the river beside the National Liberal Club.
notes: Archer and Green, 1884-87. Heights approximate (?).

name: Deptford Power Station
style_hint: Ferranti's pioneering riverside station - a plain brick hall built to carry 10,000-volt alternators, the first central high-voltage power station in the world.
notes: Sebastian de Ferranti for the London Electric Supply Corporation, generating from 1889; rebuilt as Deptford East and West stations, peak output in the 1950s, closed 1972 and demolished. Dimensions estimated (?).

name: Fulham Railway Bridge (Putney Railway Bridge)
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Opened 3 June 1889, designed by William Jacomb (Brunel's former assistant) and built by Head Wrightson for the London and South Western Railway. 418 m total with five river spans covering 301 m. Lattice girder construction. Carries the London Underground District line between Putney Bridge and East Putney, with a public footway on the downstream (east) side. Refurbished 1995-97. Colloquially 'the Iron Bridge'; it has no official name. Width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Savoy Hotel
style_hint: The first luxury hotel in Britain with electric light and lifts throughout; tall river-front block above the Embankment, and a 1929 Art Deco stainless-steel entrance canopy and sign on the Strand
notes: Built on the site of the Savoy Palace precinct. Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Teddington Lock Footbridges
style_hint: Light pedestrian deck on slender supports.
notes: A pair of iron footbridges designed by G. Pooley, built 1887-89 with money raised by local subscription and opened in 1889. The southern bridge is a suspension span over the weir stream from Teddington to a small island; the northern bridge is an iron girder span from the island over the lock cut to Ham on the Surrey bank. Both Grade II listed since 3 October 2005. Maintained by Richmond upon Thames Council. This is the tidal limit of the Thames. Length given is the combined crossing including the island; individual span lengths, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Battersea Bridge
style_hint: Cast- or wrought-iron arch ribs springing from stone piers, with iron spandrel tracery.
notes: Five cast iron arches on granite piers designed by Sir Joseph Bazalgette, opened 21 July 1890. 725 ft 6 in (221.13 m) long, 40 ft (12 m) wide, longest span 163 ft (50 m). The narrowest and one of the busiest road bridges in central London; frequently struck by river traffic. Carries the A3220. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Bankside Power Station (original)
style_hint: Low brick generating hall with a row of slim round chimneys on the Southwark bank, built by the City of London Electric Lighting Company opposite St Paul's.
notes: Generated from 1891; demolished in stages 1953-59 for Giles Gilbert Scott's replacement. Dimensions estimated (?).

name: HM Prison Wormwood Scrubs
style_hint: Built by convict labour on the telegraph-pole plan: four parallel cell blocks side by side rather than radial, with a red-brick gatehouse of twin towers bearing medallions of Howard and Fry
notes: Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Imperial Institute, South Kensington
style_hint: Long Renaissance range of Portland stone with copper-domed end turrets and a tall central campanile, part of the Albertopolis museum quarter.
notes: T. E. Colcutt, 1887-93, for the Colonial and Indian Exhibition's successor. The east and west wings were demolished 1957-67 for Imperial College; only the campanile (Queen's Tower) survives. Coordinates are those of the surviving tower; the wings ran east-west from it. Facade bearing (?).

name: Queen's Tower, Imperial College
style_hint: Free-standing Portland stone campanile of 287 ft with an open belfry stage and a copper-covered dome and lantern.
notes: Central tower of the Imperial Institute (T. E. Colcutt, 1893), 287 ft (87 m) high with 325 steps; left standing alone when the Institute was demolished 1957-67 and underpinned 1966-68.

name: Richmond Lock and Footbridge
style_hint: Light pedestrian deck on slender supports.
notes: Half-tide lock, weir and footbridge opened 19 May 1894 by the Duke of York (later George V), built to hold water upstream after the removal of Old London Bridge lowered the tidal river. 250 ft (76.2 m) long, 26 ft 8 in (8.1 m) wide, with five ornate metal arches. Three vertical steel sluice gates each weigh 32 tons and measure 66 ft by 12 ft; they are raised into the footbridge superstructure at high tide. Chief engineer F. G. M. Stoney, ironwork by Ransomes & Rapier of Ipswich. The only Thames lock operated by the Port of London Authority. Grade II* listed. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Tower Bridge
style_hint: Two Gothic-clad steel towers 65 m high on massive piers, carrying twin high-level walkways at 43 m; between them a 61 m bascule span that lifts in two leaves; suspension side spans to the abutments; total 244 m
notes: Combined bascule and suspension bridge, engineer John Wolfe Barry with architect Horace Jones. Construction from 22 April 1886, opened 30 June 1894. Total length 940 ft (290 m) including abutments; central bascule span 200 ft (61 m); towers 65 m high. Clearance 8.6 m (29 ft) above high water when closed, 42.5 m (135 ft) when open. Steel frame clad in Cornish granite and Portland stone. High-level walkways converted from cantilever to suspension form in 1960. Deck height above mean water estimated from the quoted high-water clearance (?). || from landmark fragment: Steel frame clad in Cornish granite and Portland stone to harmonise with the Tower of London. Bascules originally hydraulic (steam), electrified 1976.

name: Barnes Railway Bridge
style_hint: Bridge (rail lattice).
notes: Built 1894-95 to a design by Edward Andrews, contractor Head, Wrightson & Co, alongside and downstream of Locke's 1849 arches which remain in place. Three spans of wrought iron bowstring girders on extended piers and abutments, with a 2.4 m wide pedestrian footpath. Carries the Hounslow Loop line. Grade II listed 1983. Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Hotel Cecil, Strand
style_hint: Immense French Renaissance pile of terracotta and brick stepping down to the Embankment gardens, with 800 rooms - the largest hotel in Europe when it opened.
notes: Built 1890-96 by Perry and Reed for Jabez Balfour; demolished 1930 apart from the Strand frontage, and Shell Mex House built on the site 1931. Coordinates are those of Shell Mex House. Dimensions estimated (?).

name: Watkin's Tower, Wembley Park
style_hint: Squat iron lattice stump of eight legs carrying a single viewing platform - the first stage of a tower meant to beat the Eiffel Tower, abandoned at a fifth of its planned height.
notes: Sir Edward Watkin's 'Great Tower of London', designed for 358 m; first stage opened to the public in 1896 at about 47 m, closed 1902 after the foundations subsided, demolished 1907. Wembley Stadium now stands on the site. Footprint of the leg spread approximate (?).

name: Tate Britain (National Gallery of British Art)
