style_hint: Sidney R. J. Smith's Portland stone gallery on the site of Millbank Penitentiary: a hexastyle Corinthian portico under a pediment, low central dome, top-lit galleries; Duveen sculpture galleries 1937
notes: Built on part of the Millbank Penitentiary site. Dome height approximate?

name: Marylebone station
style_hint: Modest red-brick and terracotta Domestic Revival terminus with a porte-cochere of iron and glass linking it to the Great Central Hotel, behind a pair of low ridge-and-furrow train sheds.
notes: Opened 15 March 1899 as the London terminus of the Great Central Main Line, the last main-line terminus built in London; the adjacent Great Central Hotel is 1899 by Robert Edis.

name: Prudential Assurance Building, Holborn
style_hint: Cliff of blood-red Accrington brick and terracotta in Waterhouse's Gothic, with gables, oriels and a gate tower opening into the courtyard of Waterhouse Square.
notes: Alfred Waterhouse from 1879, extended by him and by his son Paul to 1901 on the site of Furnival's Inn. Tower height approximate (?).

name: Kew Bridge (King Edward VII Bridge)
style_hint: Masonry arch bridge with rusticated voussoirs, cutwater piers and a balustraded parapet.
notes: Officially the King Edward VII Bridge, opened 20 May 1903 by Edward VII. Designed by John Wolfe-Barry and Cuthbert Arthur Brereton. 1,182 ft (360 m) long, 75 ft (23 m) wide, three granite arches (Kemnay Quarry, Aberdeenshire), largest span 133 ft. Carries the A205 South Circular between Hounslow and Richmond upon Thames. Grade II listed 1983. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Westminster Cathedral
style_hint: J. F. Bentley, Neo-Byzantine in banded red brick and Portland stone: the widest nave in England (18 m) under three saucer domes, an apsidal sanctuary, and a detached square campanile, St Edward's Tower, 87 m, with a small dome and cross
notes: Campanile 273 ft / 87 m. Interior mosaics still unfinished.

name: Harrods
style_hint: Stephen Alfred's whole-block department store faced in pink Doulton terracotta, heavy Edwardian Baroque with domes, cupolas and an ornate skyline; lit at night by 11,500 bulbs
notes: Built in stages 1894-1905, extended to 1930s. Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Lots Road Power Station
style_hint: Long steel-framed brick generating hall with a giant arcade of round-headed windows, originally crowned by four chimneys of 275 ft - built to electrify the Underground.
notes: Built 1902-05 for the Underground Electric Railways Company of London; two of the four chimneys were removed and the others cut down when it converted to oil and gas in 1963-69. Closed 21 October 2002 and now converted to flats. Original chimney height 84 m (?).

name: Greenwich Power Station
style_hint: Massive steel-framed brick hall on the Thames just east of the Royal Naval College, with four tall chimneys and a coal jetty; built to power London's trams.
notes: Built 1902-10 for the London County Council tramways, generating from 1906; the four chimneys were shortened in the 1960s. Still a standby station for the Underground. Original chimney height approximate (?).

name: The Ritz Hotel
style_hint: London's first major steel-framed building, clad in Norwegian granite and Portland stone as a Parisian Beaux-Arts block with a Piccadilly arcade at street level and a green copper mansard roof
notes: Dimensions from map inspection?

name: University College Hospital (Cruciform Building)
style_hint: Bright red brick and terracotta cross-plan block with four diagonal wings meeting at a domed octagonal centre, gabled and turreted in Waterhouse's hardest Gothic.
notes: Alfred Waterhouse, 1897-1906, funded by Sir John Blundell Maple; now the UCL Cruciform Building. Heights approximate (?).

name: Vauxhall Bridge
style_hint: Cast- or wrought-iron arch ribs springing from stone piers, with iron spandrel tracery.
notes: Five steel arches on granite piers, designed by Sir Alexander Binnie and modified by Sir Maurice Fitzmaurice; opened 26 May 1906 by the Prince of Wales. 809 ft (247 m) long, 80 ft (24 m) wide. The first Thames bridge to carry trams. Eight large bronze figures by Alfred Drury and Frederick Pomeroy added on the piers in 1907. Grade II* listed 2008. Carries the A202. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Central Criminal Court (Old Bailey)
style_hint: Portland stone Edwardian Baroque block on the site of Newgate gaol, with a rusticated base, giant Ionic order and a green copper dome carrying the gilded figure of Justice with sword and scales.
notes: Edward William Mountford, built 1902-07 on the cleared site of Newgate Prison and opened by Edward VII on 27 February 1907; dome and statue about 67 m above the pavement (?). Bombed 1941 and repaired; a large extension added 1972.

name: White City Stadium
style_hint: Oval concrete-and-steel arena with a banked cycle track, running track and a swimming pool inside the infield, half-roofed by a curved cantilever awning; capacity about 68,000.
notes: Built in ten months by J. J. Webster for the 1908 Summer Olympics as part of the Franco-British Exhibition; hosted the first 26 mile 385 yard marathon finish, greyhound racing from 1927 and a 1966 World Cup match. Demolished 1985 for BBC White City. Original capacity often given as 93,000.

name: Selfridges, Oxford Street
style_hint: Daniel Burnham's American steel-framed store brought to London: a colossal Ionic colonnade running the length of Oxford Street on a deep plinth of plate-glass windows, flat cornice, the Queen of Time clock over the door
notes: Extended westward to its full length by 1928.

name: Twickenham Stadium
style_hint: Rugby ground built on a market garden, now an enclosed three-tier bowl with a continuous translucent roof about 49 m high; capacity 82,000.
notes: Opened October 1909 with two covered stands; wholly rebuilt in stages 1990-2006. Modelled height is a compromise between the 1909 stands and the present 49 m bowl (?).

name: Victoria and Albert Museum
style_hint: Aston Webb's Portland stone front on Cromwell Road of 1899-1909, with a domed and open-crowned lantern tower over the entrance shaped like an imperial crown; behind it the earlier iron-and-glass South Kensington Museum ranges of 1857-1884 round the Italianate garden quadrangle
notes: Museum founded 1852, on site from 1857 (the 'Brompton Boilers'). Tower height approximate?

name: Crosby Hall, Chelsea (re-erected)
style_hint: The same 15th-century hall, stone by stone, now set on Cheyne Walk as the north range of a large modern Tudor-revival courtyard house of red brick and stone with mullioned windows and tall chimneys built around it from the 1990s.
notes: Moved five miles and re-erected 1910 on part of Sir Thomas More's former Chelsea garden; at least 1500 inventoried pieces were transported. Orientation on the Chelsea site is a rough estimate?

name: Michelin House, Fulham Road
style_hint: Small Art Nouveau showroom of white faience with stained-glass Bibendum panels, tyre-shaped cupolas at the corners and a mosaic floor - a piece of pure advertising architecture.
notes: Francois Espinasse for Michelin, opened 20 January 1911; extended 1922, restored 1985 by Conran and Octopus.

name: Victoria Memorial
style_hint: Marble pylon with seated Queen Victoria facing the Mall, gilded bronze Winged Victory on top, ~25 m, in a circular stepped basin and roundabout
notes: Height approximate?

name: Admiralty Arch
style_hint: Aston Webb's curved Portland stone screen closing the Mall at Trafalgar Square: five arches (the central one only opened for state occasions), a concave facade of offices above, part of the Queen Victoria Memorial scheme
notes: Dimensions from map inspection?

name: Arsenal Stadium (Highbury)
style_hint: Tight rectangular ground wedged into terraced streets, its East and West Stands (1936 and 1932) Art Deco cliffs of white concrete with curved corner staircases and marble halls.
notes: Opened 6 September 1913 on the playing fields of St John's College; Claude Waterlow Ferrier's West Stand 1932 and East Stand 1936. Last match 7 May 2006; the stands were converted into flats as Highbury Square, the pitch becoming a garden.

name: Buckingham Palace east front (Aston Webb)
style_hint: Portland stone Beaux-Arts screen front of three storeys with a central pedimented bay and giant Corinthian pilasters, replacing Blore's decayed Caen stone facade.
notes: Refacing of the existing east range in 13 weeks in summer 1913, not a new mass - render as a facade overlay on buckingham_palace rather than a free-standing volume. Depth given is nominal (?).

name: King George V Dock
style_hint: Last of the Royal Docks, dug south of the Royal Albert with a deep entrance lock able to take the largest liners of the day.
notes: Opened by George V on 8 July 1921; closed 1981. Now flanked by London City Airport.

name: Southwark Bridge
style_hint: Cast- or wrought-iron arch ribs springing from stone piers, with iron spandrel tracery.
notes: Steel arch bridge designed by architect Ernest George and engineer Basil Mott, built by Sir William Arrol & Co. Opened by King George V on 6 June 1921. Five spans, longest 240 ft (73.2 m). Carries the A300. Grade II listed; maintained by Bridge House Estates for the City of London Corporation. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: County Hall
style_hint: Edwardian Baroque civic palace in Portland stone with a broad concave crescent to the river, a rusticated base, giant columns and steep pantiled French roofs.
notes: Ralph Knott, begun 1911 and opened by George V on 17 July 1922; north and south blocks added 1936-39 and 1963-74. Headquarters of the LCC and then the GLC until 1986; now a hotel, aquarium and gallery. Orientation follows the river crescent (?).

name: Waterloo station (rebuilt)
style_hint: The largest station in Britain: a broad ridge-and-furrow steel roof over 21 platforms and a 240 m curving concourse, entered under the Victory Arch war memorial of 1922; the arched glass Waterloo International shed by Grimshaw added along the west side 1993
notes: Waterloo International (Eurostar) 1993-2007, reopened for domestic use 2018.

name: Wembley Stadium (Empire Stadium)
style_hint: Concrete bowl behind a white ferro-concrete facade with the two domed Twin Towers, built for the British Empire Exhibition in 300 days.
notes: Opened 28 April 1923 with the 'White Horse' FA Cup Final; roofed all round 1963, hosted the 1948 Olympics and the 1966 World Cup Final. Demolished 2002-03, the Twin Towers coming down in February 2003. Towers about 38 m (126 ft).

name: Croydon Airport terminal
style_hint: Britain's first purpose-built airport terminal: a low white neoclassical block with a stepped central control tower, the Aerodrome Hotel opposite and a row of curved-roof hangars behind.
notes: The aerodrome opened 1920 with temporary buildings on Plough Lane; the permanent terminal on Purley Way opened 2 May 1928 and was the base of Imperial Airways. Closed 30 September 1959; the terminal survives as Airport House. Well south of the main scene.

name: Firestone Tyre Factory, Brentford
style_hint: Art Deco factory frontage on the Great West Road in white faience with a colonnade of stylised Egyptian columns and coloured faience friezes.
notes: Wallis, Gilbert and Partners, 1928. Demolished over the August bank holiday of 1980, days before it was to be listed - the destruction that led directly to the listing of most surviving interwar factories.

name: Broadcasting House
style_hint: Art Deco liner in Portland stone with a curved prow pointing down Regent Street, rounded corners, ribbon windows and Eric Gill's Prospero and Ariel over the door.
notes: G. Val Myer, first broadcast 15 March 1932, opened 15 May 1932. Extended by John McAslan's east wing and piazza 2005-13.

name: Daily Express Building, Fleet Street
style_hint: Streamline Moderne curtain wall of black vitrolite and clear glass with chromium strips, wrapped round rounded corners - the first glass curtain wall in London, with a dazzling Art Deco lobby.
notes: Ellis and Clarke with Owen Williams, 1930-32. Offices behind the facade wholly rebuilt in the 1990s.

name: Lambeth Bridge
style_hint: Cast- or wrought-iron arch ribs springing from stone piers, with iron spandrel tracery.
notes: Five-span steel arch bridge by engineer Sir George Humphreys with architects Sir Reginald Blomfield and G. Topham Forrest, built by Dorman Long; opened by King George V on 19 July 1932. Painted red to match the benches of the House of Lords. Obelisks at each end topped with stone pine cones (popularly but wrongly called pineapples). Grade II listed 2008. Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Shell Mex House (80 Strand)
style_hint: Broad Art Deco stepped block facing the river, its centre rising to a tower carrying the largest clock face in London ('Big Benzene').
notes: Frances Milton Cashmore, opened 1932 on the site of the Hotel Cecil, whose Strand facade was kept; 58 m (190 ft) tall, 12 floors. Renamed Eighty Strand.

name: Chiswick Bridge
style_hint: Bridge (concrete beam).
notes: Opened 3 July 1933 by the Prince of Wales on the same day as Twickenham Bridge and the rebuilt Hampton Court Bridge. Architect Sir Herbert Baker, engineer Alfred Dryland. 606 ft (185 m) long, 70 ft (21 m) wide, five spans (three over the river, two over towpaths), longest span 150 ft (46 m); reinforced concrete faced with 3,400 tons of Portland stone. At completion the longest concrete span over the Thames. Near the Boat Race finish. Structurally a concrete arch; kind set to concrete_beam as the nearest category (?). Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Hampton Court Bridge
style_hint: Bridge (concrete beam).
notes: Designed by W. P. Robinson with Sir Edwin Lutyens as consulting architect; opened 3 July 1933 by the Prince of Wales on the same day as Twickenham and Chiswick bridges. Three wide reinforced concrete arches faced in red brick and Portland stone to complement Hampton Court Palace opposite. Carries the A309 between East Molesey (Surrey) and Hampton Court. Grade II listed 1952; maintained by Surrey County Council. Structurally a concrete arch; kind set to concrete_beam as the nearest category (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Hoover Building, Perivale
style_hint: Long white faience factory front on the Western Avenue with a symmetrical centrepiece of Egyptian-Aztec colour, sunburst glazing bars and green and red faience banding.
notes: Wallis, Gilbert and Partners, 1932-33; production ended 1982, converted to a Tesco and flats. Coordinates approximate (?).

name: Twickenham Bridge
style_hint: Bridge (concrete beam).
notes: Opened 3 July 1933 by the Prince of Wales. Architect Maxwell Ayrton, engineer Alfred Dryland. Three reinforced concrete arches on concrete piers with Art Deco bronze cover plates, balustrades and lamps; the first reinforced concrete bridge in the UK to use three permanent hinges to accommodate thermal movement. Carries the A316 Chertsey Road between Richmond and St Margarets. Site of the UK's first Gatso speed camera in 1992. Grade II* listed 2008. Structurally a concrete arch; kind set to concrete_beam as the nearest category (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Isokon Flats, Lawn Road
style_hint: White reinforced-concrete deck-access block of minimum flats with open access galleries and cantilevered stairs - the first modernist block of flats in Britain.
notes: Wells Coates for Jack and Molly Pritchard, 1934. Residents included Gropius, Breuer, Moholy-Nagy and Agatha Christie. Restored 2003.

name: Wembley Arena (Empire Pool)
style_hint: Long hall spanned by exposed reinforced-concrete parabolic arches, built round an Olympic-size swimming pool that was later floored over.
notes: Owen Williams, opened 1934 as the Empire Pool for the Empire Games; the pool was covered in 1948. Refurbished 2005-06.

name: Alexandra Palace television mast
style_hint: Slender steel lattice mast rising from the south-east tower of the palace, carrying the aerials of the world's first regular high-definition television service.
notes: Erected 1935 for the BBC Television Service, on air from 2 November 1936; 215 ft (66 m) tall. Position on the palace roof approximate (?).

name: Battersea Power Station A
style_hint: Brick cathedral of power by Giles Gilbert Scott: a steel frame clad in fluted brickwork with Art Deco detail, a tall turbine hall and boiler house, and two fluted concrete chimneys at the north and south ends.
notes: Built 1929-35 (A station); with B station it formed the largest brick building in Europe. Chimneys about 103 m tall. Closed 1975; the four chimneys were dismantled and rebuilt in replica 2014-17.

name: Bush House, Aldwych
style_hint: Portland stone Beaux-Arts block closing the vista north up Kingsway with a monumental portal of paired Corinthian columns carrying the figures of Anglo-American friendship.
notes: Harvey Wiley Corbett for Irving T. Bush; centre block 1923-25, wings completed 1935. Home of the BBC World Service 1941-2012, now part of King's College London.

name: Highpoint I, Highgate
style_hint: Crisp white double-cruciform slab of eight storeys on the Highgate ridge, its plan a cross of four wings, praised by Le Corbusier as a milestone of modern architecture.
notes: Berthold Lubetkin and Tecton, 1933-35; Highpoint II followed in 1938.

name: Imperial War Museum
style_hint: The truncated centre block of the old Bethlem hospital: portico, copper dome, and a pair of 15-inch naval guns on the lawn in front
notes: Museum founded 1917, at Crystal Palace then South Kensington before moving here.

name: Chelsea Bridge
style_hint: Suspension bridge: chains or cables slung between masonry or iron towers over a light deck.
notes: The first self-anchored suspension bridge in Britain, with the suspension cables anchored into the deck rather than into ground anchorages; designed by G. Topham Forrest and E. P. Wheeler for the LCC. Opened 6 May 1937. 698 ft (213 m) long, 64 ft (20 m) wide with a 40 ft roadway and cantilevered 12 ft pavements; central span 332 ft (101 m). All-steel construction. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Dolphin Square, Pimlico
style_hint: Vast brick quadrangle of 1,250 flats in thirteen linked ten-storey blocks round a private garden - the largest self-contained block of flats in Europe when built.
notes: Gordon Jeeves for Costain, 1935-37, on the site of an army clothing depot.

name: Earls Court Exhibition Centre
style_hint: Art moderne white concrete slab with a curved corner drum and vertical fins, wrapped round the largest reinforced-concrete exhibition hall in Europe over the District line tracks.
notes: C. Howard Crane, built 1935-37 on the site of the 1887 exhibition grounds; Earls Court Two added 1991. Demolition 2014-17. Footprint of the 1937 hall approximate (?).

name: Odeon Leicester Square
style_hint: Slab of polished black granite with a tall fin tower and neon name sign, the last and grandest of Oscar Deutsch's Odeons.
notes: Harry Weedon and Andrew Mather, opened 2 November 1937. Fin height approximate (?).

name: Senate House, University of London
style_hint: Charles Holden's cliff of white Portland stone: a stepped, almost windowless ziggurat tower of 19 floors rising above long low wings, deliberately built to last 500 years.
notes: Built 1932-37 as the first phase of an uncompleted scheme; 210 ft (64 m) high, 19 floors. Used by the Ministry of Information in the war and the model for Orwell's Ministry of Truth.

name: Du Cane Court, Balham
style_hint: Long streamlined Art Deco block of 676 flats in brown brick with curved corner balconies and Crittall windows, laid out on a symmetrical splayed plan.
notes: G. Kay Green, 1935-38; the largest privately owned block of flats under one roof in Europe at the time.

name: Bank of England (Herbert Baker rebuild)
style_hint: Herbert Baker kept Soane's blank screen wall and raised a seven-storey stone block inside and above it, with a colonnaded upper front and a stepped attic; three basement levels of gold vaults
notes: Height above the old wall approximate?

name: Wandsworth Bridge
style_hint: Bridge (cantilever).
notes: Three-span steel cantilever bridge by Sir Thomas Peirson Frank, opened 25 September 1940 at a cost of about GBP 503,000. 650 ft (200 m) long, 60 ft (18 m) wide, clearance 39 ft (11.9 m) at lowest astronomical tide - deck_height_m here is referred to mean water level, so lower (?). Painted dull blue as wartime camouflage and still blue. Carries the A217; about 53,000 vehicles a day. Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Waterloo Bridge
style_hint: Bridge (concrete beam).
notes: Designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, construction begun 1937. Reinforced concrete box girders clad in Portland stone, five spans, longest 233 ft (71 m). Partially opened 11 March 1942 and fully complete in 1945 (formally opened 10 December 1945); birth year given as 1942 for the first opening, 1945 for full completion (?). Built largely by a female workforce, hence 'The Ladies' Bridge'. Grade II* listed 1981. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Heathrow Airport
style_hint: Two parallel east-west runways with a central terminal island reached by a tunnel, ringed by aprons, hangars and cargo sheds.
notes: Opened as London Airport on 31 May 1946 on the site of the Great West Aerodrome; the first permanent terminal (Europa, later Terminal 2) opened 1955. Footprint is the whole airfield envelope, not a building.

name: Dome of Discovery, Festival of Britain
style_hint: Flattened saucer of aluminium 365 ft across on a ring of raking lattice struts - the largest dome in the world when built, and the centrepiece of the South Bank exhibition.
notes: Ralph Tubbs with Freeman Fox, 1949-51; 111 m diameter, about 27 m high. Demolished with the rest of the Festival site in 1952 apart from the Royal Festival Hall.

name: Royal Festival Hall
style_hint: LCC Architects' Department: the 'egg in a box' - a 2,900-seat auditorium suspended within a rectangular envelope of glass and Portland stone, with public foyers wrapping round and under it and a long river-facing glazed wall
notes: The only permanent building of the 1951 Festival of Britain South Bank site. River front remodelled 1962-65.

name: Skylon, Festival of Britain
style_hint: Slender cigar of steel lattice clad in aluminium louvres, held nose-up on cables between three slanting struts so that it appeared to float above the ground with no visible support.
notes: Powell, Moya and Felix Samuely for the Festival of Britain, May-September 1951; cut up for scrap on Churchill's orders in 1952. Overall height above ground about 90 m, the cigar itself about 76 m (?).

name: Battersea Power Station B
style_hint: Mirror image of the A station completed to the east after the war, giving the building its famous four-chimney upturned-table silhouette.
notes: Begun 1944, completed 1955; the whole station closed 31 October 1983. Chimneys about 103 m. Positions of the A and B halves are split by hand from the single Wikipedia coordinate (?).

name: Crystal Palace transmitting station
style_hint: Steel lattice tower with a broad base tapering to a slender aerial mast, standing on the highest ground in south London on the site of Baird's 1933 television station.
notes: Built 1954-56 for BBC television; 219 m tall and the eighth-tallest structure in London. The main transmitter for Greater London.

name: Golden Lane Estate (Great Arthur House)
style_hint: Sixteen-storey slab of yellow, red and blue panels with a boldly cantilevered concrete canopy and roof garden, standing over low maisonette ranges round courts.
notes: Chamberlin, Powell and Bon's competition-winning estate, 1952-62; Great Arthur House 1957 was briefly the tallest residential block in Britain at about 55 m (?). Coordinates approximate.

name: Alton Estate, Roehampton
style_hint: Five eleven-storey Corbusian slab blocks on pilotis marching across the parkland of Downshire Field, with point blocks and terraces among mature trees.
notes: LCC Architect's Department, Alton East 1955 and Alton West 1958 - the most admired public housing scheme of the period. Footprint is the group envelope, not one block (?).

name: Shell Centre, South Bank
style_hint: Heavy Portland stone-clad tower of 26 storeys with a clock stage near the top, rising from long stripped-classical wings either side of the Hungerford railway viaduct.
notes: Howard Robertson, 1957-62; the Upstream Building tower is 107 m and was briefly the tallest office building in Britain. Downstream Building replaced by new towers 2016-21.

name: Bankside Power Station (Scott)
style_hint: Giles Gilbert Scott's brick monolith facing St Paul's across the river: a long low turbine hall and boiler house with a single square central chimney of 99 m, deliberately kept lower than the cathedral dome.
notes: Designed 1947, built in two phases 1947-52 and 1959-63 as an oil-fired station; closed 31 October 1981. 4.2 million bricks; chimney 99 m.

name: London Hilton on Park Lane
style_hint: Y-plan 28-storey hotel slab in exposed concrete and glass overlooking Hyde Park, controversial for overlooking the gardens of Buckingham Palace.
notes: William B. Tabler, 1960-63; 101 m, 28 floors. The first tower to break the West End skyline.

name: Millbank Tower
style_hint: Slim glass-and-aluminium curtain-walled slab of 32 storeys with a shallow curved plan, standing free on a riverside podium - the tallest building in Britain on completion.
notes: Ronald Ward and Partners, 1960-63, built as Vickers Tower; 118 m and 32 storeys.

name: New Zealand House, Haymarket
style_hint: Glass curtain-walled tower of 18 storeys on a low glazed podium at the corner of Pall Mall and the Haymarket - one of the first modern towers in the West End.
notes: Robert Matthew, Johnson-Marshall and Partners, 1957-63; about 68 m (?).

name: BT Tower (Post Office Tower)
style_hint: Cylindrical concrete shaft of 20 m diameter with a glazed collar of microwave dish galleries near the top and a revolving restaurant, crowned by an aerial mast.
notes: Eric Bedford, 1961-64, opened to the public 1966; 177 m to the roof, 189 m with the aerial rigging. The tallest building in Britain 1964-80; officially secret until 1993.

name: Elephant and Castle shopping centre
style_hint: Squat pink-painted concrete box of three levels wrapped by a roundabout and subways - the first covered shopping mall in Europe.
notes: Boissevain and Osmond, opened 1965. Closed 24 September 2020 and demolished 2021 for the Elephant and Castle Town Centre scheme. Coordinates approximate (?).

name: Centre Point
style_hint: Sculptural 34-storey slab of precast concrete lattice panels shaped like stacked hourglasses, straddling the St Giles Circus road junction on stilts.
notes: Richard Seifert for Harry Hyams, 1963-66; 117 m. Notorious for standing empty through the 1970s; converted to flats 2015-18.

name: Balfron Tower
style_hint: The prototype for Trellick: a 26-storey concrete slab with a separate lift tower joined by access bridges, on the edge of the Blackwall Tunnel approach.
notes: Erno Goldfinger for the LCC/GLC, 1965-67; about 84 m. Goldfinger himself lived in flat 130 for two months. Grade II* listed; refurbished for private sale 2015-22.

name: Queen Elizabeth Hall and Purcell Room
style_hint: Board-marked concrete Brutalist assembly of blank boxes, ventilation stacks and elevated walkways, with the Purcell Room tucked beneath.
notes: LCC/GLC Architect's Department (Hubert Bennett), opened 1 March 1967. Refurbished 2015-18.

name: Euston station (rebuilt)
style_hint: Low horizontal slab: a 200 m glazed curtain-walled concourse box with a flat roof on a black granite plinth, set behind an open piazza and flanked by three office blocks.
notes: Rebuilt 1962-68 by British Rail (R. L. Moorcroft) for West Coast electrification and opened 14 October 1968. Height of the concourse block approximate (?).

name: Hayward Gallery
style_hint: Windowless concrete galleries stepping in interlocking blocks, top-lit by 66 glazed pyramids on the roof.
notes: GLC Architect's Department, opened 9 July 1968. Refurbished 2015-18.

name: Heathrow Terminal 1
style_hint: Rectilinear concrete and glass terminal on the central island, opened by the Queen as the largest short-haul terminal in western Europe.
notes: Opened 17 April 1969 (building complete 1968); closed 29 June 2015 and demolished for the Terminal 2 expansion. The 1955 control tower stood nearby; the present 87 m tower dates from 2007.

name: Ronan Point, Canning Town
style_hint: Twenty-two-storey system-built tower of large precast concrete panels bolted together, one of nine in the Freemasons Estate.
notes: Completed March 1968; on 16 May 1968 a gas explosion on the 18th floor blew out load-bearing panels and collapsed one whole corner, killing four. Demolished carefully in 1986 as a forensic exercise. Height about 64 m (?).

name: Space House (One Kemble Street)
style_hint: Cylindrical 17-storey drum of precast concrete Y-shaped mullions, linked by a bridge to a matching slab - Seifert's circular counterpart to Centre Point.
notes: Richard Seifert for Harry Hyams, 1964-68. Height approximate (?).

name: Commercial Union Tower (St Helen's)
style_hint: Miesian black steel and bronze-glass tower hung from a central core and standing on an open plaza, the first City building to break the 100 m line.
notes: Gollins, Melvin, Ward and Partners, 1964-69; 118 m, 28 storeys. Gutted by the 1992 Baltic Exchange bomb and rebuilt; renamed St Helen's.

name: Euston Tower
style_hint: Plain 36-storey curtain-walled slab on the Euston Road, part of the Euston Centre commercial scheme.
notes: Sidney Kaye, Eric Firmin and Partners, 1970; 124 m. Slated for redevelopment.

name: King's Reach Tower
style_hint: Slender 30-storey concrete-and-glass tower built for IPC Magazines, long the tallest building on the South Bank.
notes: Richard Seifert, 1972; 111 m. Extended upward and reclad 2012-16 as South Bank Tower - the death date marks that transformation, not demolition.

name: Robin Hood Gardens
style_hint: Two long curving concrete slabs of ten and seven storeys with 'streets in the sky' access decks, facing each other across an artificial green mound.
notes: Alison and Peter Smithson, 1968-72. Listing refused three times; demolition began 2017 and a facade fragment went to the V&A. Death date is the start of demolition, completed 2025 (?).

name: Trellick Tower
style_hint: Brutalist slab of 31 storeys with a detached lift and service tower linked by bridges every third floor, its boiler house cantilevered out near the top.
notes: Erno Goldfinger for the GLC, 1968-72; about 98 m. Grade II* listed 1998.

name: Cromwell Tower, Barbican
style_hint: Triangular-plan Brutalist residential tower of 42 storeys in pick-hammered concrete, with projecting balconies at the corners and a fretted concrete crown.
notes: Chamberlin, Powell and Bon, completed 1973; 123 m, 42 storeys - the tallest residential buildings in Europe when built. Coordinates estimated within the Barbican Estate (?).

name: London Bridge
style_hint: Bridge (concrete beam).
notes: Prestressed concrete box girder, three spans, longest span 104 m. Architect Lord Holford, engineers Mott, Hay and Anderson. Built 1967-72 on the site of Rennie's bridge and opened by Elizabeth II on 16 March 1973. Cost GBP 4 million, funded by Bridge House Estates. Deck height above mean water approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Guy's Tower (Tower Wing)
style_hint: Concrete-framed hospital tower of 34 floors with a stepped plant-room crown, reclad 2013-14 in coloured glazed panels.
notes: Watkins Gray International, completed 1974 at 142.6 m; the tallest hospital building in the world. Recladding in 2014 took it to 148.65 m (487.7 ft).

name: Heygate Estate, Walworth
style_hint: Long slab blocks of grey precast concrete up to twelve storeys, linked by elevated walkways round green space, holding 1,200 dwellings.
notes: Tim Tinker for Southwark, 1970-74; emptied from 2007 and demolished 2011-14 for the Elephant Park scheme. Footprint is the estate envelope (?).

name: Lauderdale Tower, Barbican
style_hint: Second of the three identical triangular Barbican towers of bush-hammered concrete.
notes: Chamberlin, Powell and Bon, completed 1974; 123 m, 43 storeys. Coordinates estimated (?).

name: National Theatre
style_hint: Stacked horizontal terraces of board-marked concrete stepping down to the river, with two square fly towers rising over the Olivier and Lyttelton auditoria.
notes: Denys Lasdun, 1969-76; opened in stages from 16 March 1976. Fly tower height approximate (?).

name: Shakespeare Tower, Barbican
style_hint: Last of the three Barbican towers, closing the estate to the east above the lakeside terraces.
notes: Chamberlin, Powell and Bon, completed 1976; 123 m, 44 storeys. Coordinates estimated (?).

name: Aylesbury Estate, Walworth
style_hint: Enormous system-built estate of long slabs up to fourteen storeys linked by walkways, once holding around 10,000 people - one of the largest in Europe.
notes: Southwark Borough Architect (Hans Peter Trenton), 1963-77. Progressive demolition and replacement since 2010 and still under way. Footprint is the estate envelope (?).

name: Alexandra Road Estate
style_hint: Two stepped white concrete terraces facing each other across a pedestrian street, the taller eight-storey block acting as an acoustic wall against the railway.
notes: Neave Brown for Camden, 1968-78; Grade II* listed 1993, the first postwar council estate to be listed.

name: Tower 42 (NatWest Tower)
style_hint: Three cantilevered chevron-plan leaves of bronze glass stacked round a central concrete core, its plan modelled on the NatWest logo.
notes: Richard Seifert, 1971-80; 183 m, 47 storeys - the tallest building in Britain 1980-90 and the first City skyscraper. Badly damaged by the 1993 Bishopsgate bomb.

name: Barbican Centre
style_hint: Largely subterranean arts complex of board-marked concrete under the estate's raised podium, with a conservatory glasshouse on the roof over the fly tower.
notes: Chamberlin, Powell and Bon, opened by the Queen 3 March 1982; concert hall, theatre, cinemas and art gallery. Height above podium approximate (?).

name: Thames Barrier
style_hint: Line of ten steel gates between nine concrete piers, each pier hooded in a shell of stainless steel shaped like a section of a boat hull.
notes: Rendel, Palmer and Tritton, built 1974-82, operational from 8 October 1982 and formally opened 8 May 1984; 520 m across the Woolwich Reach. Orientation is across the river (?).

name: Lloyd's building
style_hint: Inside-out high-tech steel: six satellite service towers of stainless-steel ducts, lifts and lavatory pods clipped round a rectangular block with a barrel-vaulted glazed atrium, and blue cranes on the roof.
notes: Richard Rogers Partnership, 1978-86; 88 m to the roof, 95.1 m with the maintenance cranes. Grade I listed in 2011, the youngest building ever so listed.

name: London City Airport
style_hint: Single short runway laid on the quay between the Royal Albert and King George V docks, with a small terminal and apron on the north side.
notes: Proposed 1981, opened 26 October 1987; runway extended 1992 and the terminal repeatedly enlarged.

name: One Canada Square
style_hint: Square stainless-steel-clad shaft of 50 storeys topped by a pyramid roof with a flashing aircraft light - the symbol of Docklands.
notes: Cesar Pelli, 1988-91; 235 m, the tallest building in Britain 1990-2010. Built over the West India Export Dock.

name: Queen Elizabeth II Bridge (Dartford Crossing)
style_hint: Suspension bridge: chains or cables slung between masonry or iron towers over a light deck.
notes: OUTSIDE FRAME - about 30 km downstream of the Thames Barrier, far east of the Hampton Court to Barrier study area; included only for completeness. Cable-stayed bridge designed by Hellmut Homberg with Halcrow as check engineer, opened by Elizabeth II on 30 October 1991 at a cost of GBP 120 million. Main span 450 m, towers 137 m high, deck about 61 m above water at the crown - deck_height_m 57.5 is a mid-span average (?). Carries four southbound lanes of the A282/M25; northbound traffic uses the two tunnels. Length 812 m is the cable-stayed structure; the whole crossing including approach viaducts is about 2,872 m (?). Structurally cable-stayed; kind set to suspension as the nearest category (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: SIS Building (MI6), Vauxhall Cross
style_hint: Cream and green ziggurat of stepped concrete terraces and bronze glass on the river bank beside Vauxhall Bridge, likened to an Aztec temple or a wedding cake.
notes: Terry Farrell, 1989-94, headquarters of the Secret Intelligence Service from 1994; hit by a rocket-propelled grenade in 2000. Height about 60 m (?) - Wikipedia gives no figure.

name: British Library, St Pancras
style_hint: Red brick liner with sloping slate roofs and a stepped piazza, its bulk deliberately low beside St Pancras, over four basement levels of bookstacks.
notes: Colin St John Wilson, designed from 1978, built 1982-97 and opened 1998 - the largest public building constructed in Britain in the 20th century.

name: Shakespeare's Globe (reconstruction)
style_hint: An academic reconstruction using period methods: green oak frame with mortice-and-tenon joints and oak pegs, lime plaster on riven laths, a 20-sided polygon of three galleries around an open yard, thrust stage with painted 'marble' columns and a heavens ceiling, and Britain's first new thatched roof since 1666 (with concealed sprinklers).
notes: Sam Wanamaker's project, opened 1997, about 230 m (750 ft) from the original Globe site because the real site lies under listed Georgian terraces. An academic approximation of the 1599 and 1614 buildings, not an exact copy. Era label 'Stuart' used only to satisfy the enum - the building is 1990s.

name: The O2 (Millennium Dome)
style_hint: Shallow white PTFE-coated fabric dome 365 m across slung from twelve 100 m steel masts on the Greenwich peninsula.
notes: Richard Rogers Partnership with Buro Happold, 1997-99, for the Millennium Experience of 2000; reopened as the O2 arena 24 June 2007. Roof 52 m at the centre, masts 100 m.

name: British Museum Great Court roof
style_hint: Foster + Partners: an undulating steel-and-glass toroidal lattice roof of 1,656 unique panes spanning the old courtyard around the drum of the Reading Room; Europe's largest covered square
notes: Roof 6,100 sq m. Height approximate?

name: ExCeL London
style_hint: Long low exhibition shed on the north quay of the Royal Victoria Dock, its roof a run of tented steel arches with two boulevard entrances.
notes: Moxley Architects, opened November 2000; Phase 2 doubled it eastward in 2010. Hosted seven sports at the 2012 Olympics and the 2020 NHS Nightingale hospital.

name: London Eye
style_hint: Cantilevered observation wheel 120 m across carrying 32 sealed glass capsules on the outside of the rim, held by an A-frame on the Jubilee Gardens bank.
notes: Marks Barfield, erected 1999 and opened to the public 9 March 2000; 135 m tall, 120 m diameter. Built as a five-year temporary structure and now permanent.

name: Millennium Bridge
style_hint: Light pedestrian deck on slender supports.
notes: Steel lateral suspension footbridge with cables below deck level ('blade of light'), by Arup, Foster + Partners and Anthony Caro. Opened 10 June 2000, closed after two days on 12 June 2000 because of synchronous lateral excitation ('wobbly bridge'), reopened 22 February 2002 after fitting 37 viscous and 52 tuned mass dampers at a cost of GBP 5 million. Three spans of 81 m, 144 m and 108 m. Classified here as footbridge although structurally a shallow suspension bridge. Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: Tate Modern
style_hint: The power station converted: the boiler house hollowed out into the vast Turbine Hall, a two-storey glass light-beam laid along the roof, and the chimney kept as the Swiss Light.
notes: Herzog and de Meuron conversion 1995-2000, opened 12 May 2000. Same fabric as bankside_power_station_1963 - render as a re-skin, not a new mass.

name: Portcullis House
style_hint: Bronze-clad parliamentary offices with heavy black ventilation chimneys round a glass-roofed courtyard, built over Westminster Underground station.
notes: Michael Hopkins and Partners, 1992-2001, opened 2001. Height approximate (?).

name: 25 Canada Square (Citigroup Centre)
style_hint: Twin of the HSBC tower on the south side of Canada Square, flat-topped in silver-grey glass and steel, 45 storeys.
notes: Cesar Pelli, 1999-2001; 200 m. With 33 Canada Square it forms the Citigroup Centre.

name: City Hall, More London
style_hint: Leaning glass ovoid tilted away from the sun to reduce solar gain, with a helical ramp winding up inside past the debating chamber.
notes: Foster and Partners, 1998-2002, opened July 2002; ten storeys, about 45 m. Home of the Greater London Authority until it moved to the Crystal at the Royal Docks in December 2021 - the building itself survives as offices.

name: 8 Canada Square (HSBC Tower)
style_hint: Flat-topped stainless-steel and glass slab of 45 storeys, one of the pair flanking One Canada Square.
notes: Foster and Partners, 1999-2002; 200 m, global headquarters of HSBC.

name: Golden Jubilee Bridges
style_hint: Light pedestrian deck on slender supports.
notes: A pair of cable-stayed pedestrian decks flanking the 1864 Hungerford railway bridge on either side, designed by Lifschutz Davidson Sandilands with WSP Group; opened 2002 and named for the Golden Jubilee of Elizabeth II. Sources give the length variously as about 300 m or 325 m (?). Coordinates are for the pair as a whole - the two decks sit roughly 20 m either side of the rail bridge centreline (?). Carry about 8.5 million pedestrians a year, London's busiest footbridges. Width per deck approximate (?). Deck height approximate (?). Deck bearing derived from the local river direction (?).

name: 30 St Mary Axe (The Gherkin)
style_hint: Tapering glass bullet on a circular plan with a diagonal steel diagrid and spiralling dark light-wells, capped by a glazed lens.
notes: Foster and Partners, 2001-03, on the site of the Baltic Exchange destroyed by the 1992 IRA bomb; 180 m, 41 storeys.

name: One Churchill Place (Barclays)
style_hint: Silver-grey 32-storey tower east of Canada Square with a projecting glazed lift wall, headquarters of Barclays.
notes: HOK International, 2001-04; 156 m.

name: Emirates Stadium
style_hint: Four-tier elliptical bowl clad in glass and polycarbonate with a curved cantilever roof, holding 60,700.
notes: Populous (HOK Sport), 2004-06, opened 22 July 2006 as Arsenal's replacement for Highbury.

name: Wembley Stadium
style_hint: Bowl of 90,000 seats with a partly retractable roof hung from a single 315 m lattice arch rising 133 m above the north side, visible across west London.
notes: Foster and Partners with Populous, 2003-07, opened 9 March 2007; the arch spans 315 m and peaks at 133 m.

name: Broadgate Tower
style_hint: Thirty-five-storey glass tower with exposed external cross-bracing, straddling the railway approach to Liverpool Street.
notes: Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, 2005-08; 164 m.

name: Heathrow Terminal 5
style_hint: Single-span wave roof of steel arches 156 m across floating over a glass-walled concourse, with two satellite piers to the south.
notes: Richard Rogers Partnership, built 2002-08 after the longest public inquiry in British history; opened 27 March 2008. Concourse 396 m long.

name: Strata SE1
style_hint: Forty-three-storey residential tower of grey and white banded glass whose sculpted top houses three 9 m wind turbines in circular openings.
notes: BFLS, 2007-10; 148 m. Won the Carbuncle Cup in 2010; the turbines rarely run.

name: Heron Tower (110 Bishopsgate)
style_hint: Stack of three-storey office villages behind a bright external steel frame, with a huge aquarium in the lobby and a glazed mast on top.
notes: Kohn Pedersen Fox, 2007-11; 202 m to the roof, 230 m with the mast - the tallest building in the City until 2020.

name: London Aquatics Centre
style_hint: Double-curved aluminium wave roof of 160 m span rising from two concrete supports over two 50 m pools and a diving pit.
notes: Zaha Hadid, 2008-11; the two temporary 'wings' of seating were removed after 2012, leaving 2,500 seats.

name: London Stadium (Olympic Stadium)
style_hint: Elliptical bowl of a permanent lower tier of concrete with a demountable lightweight steel upper tier, ringed since 2016 by the largest cantilevered roof in the world.
notes: Populous, built 2008-11 for the 2012 Olympics with 80,000 seats; converted 2013-16 to a 62,500-seat football ground for West Ham. Height approximate (?).

name: Westfield Stratford City
style_hint: Very large enclosed shopping centre of glazed malls and roof-lit atria forming the gateway between Stratford station and the Olympic Park.
notes: Opened 13 September 2011; about 175,000 sq m of retail, one of the largest urban shopping centres in Europe. Footprint approximate (?).

name: ArcelorMittal Orbit
style_hint: Tangled red steel loop of tubular members spiralling round two viewing platforms - Britain's largest piece of public art, with a slide added in 2016.
notes: Anish Kapoor with Cecil Balmond, 2010-12; 114.5 m.

name: Emirates Air Line (IFS Cloud Cable Car)
style_hint: Gondola cable car crossing the Thames on three tapered steel pylons, the tallest 87 m, carrying 34 cabins between Greenwich Peninsula and the Royal Docks.
notes: Wilkinson Eyre and Expedition Engineering, opened 28 June 2012; span about 1.1 km. Footprint is the line envelope, not a building.

name: The Shard
style_hint: Pyramidal spire of eight leaning glass shards that do not quite meet at the top, leaving a fractured open crown above the 72nd habitable floor.
notes: Renzo Piano for Sellar, 2009-12, on the site of Southwark Towers; inaugurated 5 July 2012 at 309.6 m and 87 storeys - the tallest building in the United Kingdom.

name: 122 Leadenhall Street (The Cheesegrater)
style_hint: Wedge-shaped tower whose north face rises sheer while the south face rakes back at 10 degrees to protect the view of St Paul's, carried on an exposed steel megaframe over a seven-storey open plaza.
notes: Rogers Stirk Harbour and Partners, 2011-14; 224.5 m, 48 storeys.

name: St George Wharf Tower (Vauxhall Tower)
style_hint: Cylindrical 50-storey residential tower of louvred glass with a wind turbine set into the roof; the tallest wholly residential building in Britain when finished.
notes: Broadway Malyan, 2010-14; 181 m. A helicopter struck its crane in fog in January 2013, killing two.

name: 20 Fenchurch Street (The Walkie-Talkie)
style_hint: Top-heavy tower flaring outward as it rises, its concave south facade crowned by the three-storey Sky Garden under a curved glass roof.
notes: Rafael Vinoly, 2010-14; 160 m, 38 storeys. Its concave glass focused sunlight strongly enough in 2013 to melt car trim, and it won the Carbuncle Cup in 2015.

name: Crossrail Place, Canary Wharf
style_hint: Timber lattice shell of 1,400 ETFE-cushioned panels arching over a roof garden, set in the water of the West India North Dock above the Elizabeth line box.
notes: Foster and Partners with Arup, 2009-15; the roof garden opened 2015 and the station itself in May 2022. 310 m long.

name: South Bank Tower
style_hint: The 1972 tower stripped to its frame, reclad in faceted glass and extended by eleven storeys, with a new fan-shaped block at its foot.
notes: KPF conversion for CIT, 2012-16; 155 m, 41 storeys, converted from offices to flats.

name: Tate Modern Blavatnik Building (Switch House)
style_hint: Twisted truncated pyramid of perforated brick lattice rising behind the old power station over the buried oil tanks.
notes: Herzog and de Meuron, 2010-16, opened 17 June 2016; 64.5 m, ten storeys.

name: One Blackfriars (The Vase)
style_hint: Bulging convex glass tower of 50 storeys, wider at the middle than at either end, on the south approach to Blackfriars Bridge.
notes: Simpson Haugh and Partners, 2013-18; 163 m.

name: Principal Tower, Shoreditch
style_hint: Slim 50-storey residential tower of rippling glass at the north edge of Broadgate, its plan twisting slightly as it rises.
notes: Foster and Partners, 2015-18; about 152 m (?).

name: The Scalpel (52 Lime Street)
style_hint: Sharply faceted glass wedge of angled planes, deliberately shaped to keep clear of the protected view corridor to St Paul's.
notes: Kohn Pedersen Fox for W. R. Berkley, 2015-18; 190 m, 38 storeys. The nickname came from a Financial Times article and was adopted by the developer.

name: One Park Drive
style_hint: Cylindrical 57-storey tower of stacked bands - loggia, cluster and bay flats - each band expressed differently, likened to Chicago's Marina City.
notes: Herzog and de Meuron at Wood Wharf, 2016-19; about 205 m (?), 57 storeys.

name: Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
style_hint: Steep single-tier South Stand under a glazed and clad bowl with a retractable grass pitch sliding away to reveal an artificial NFL surface beneath.
notes: Populous, 2016-19, opened 3 April 2019 on the site of White Hart Lane; 62,850 seats, about 48 m high.

name: Landmark Pinnacle
style_hint: Slender 75-storey residential shaft on Marsh Wall clad in blue-grey glass with a stepped crown - the tallest residential building in western Europe.
notes: Squire and Partners for Chalegrove Properties, 2016-20; 233 m, 75 storeys.

name: 22 Bishopsgate
style_hint: Faceted crystalline shaft of 62 storeys stepping back in a series of chamfered planes - by floor area the largest office building in the City.
notes: PLP Architecture, 2016-20, on the abandoned Pinnacle site; 278 m, the tallest building in the City of London.

name: Newfoundland
style_hint: Diamond-shaped residential tower in an exposed white external diagrid frame, tapering slightly toward the top; 58 storeys.
notes: Horden Cherry Lee with WSP, 2017-21; 220 m, 636 build-to-rent flats.

name: Battersea Power Station redevelopment
style_hint: The restored power station reopened as shops and offices with a glass lift in one rebuilt chimney, flanked by Gehry's and Foster's new residential blocks along Electric Boulevard.
notes: Restoration by WilkinsonEyre 2013-22, opened to the public 14 October 2022; the four chimneys were demolished and rebuilt in replica 2014-17. Overlaps the A and B station records - render as a re-skin plus the surrounding new blocks (?).

name: 8 Bishopsgate
style_hint: Three stacked and offset glass volumes stepping back toward the top, with a free public viewing gallery on the 50th floor.
notes: Wilkinson Eyre, 2019-23; 204 m, 50 storeys.

name: One Nine Elms City Tower
style_hint: Taller of two linked towers at Vauxhall, 57 storeys of stepped bronze-toned glass, the residential half of the scheme.
notes: Kohn Pedersen Fox for Wanda and then R&F, 2017-23; 57 storeys, about 200 m (?).

name: One Nine Elms River Tower
style_hint: Shorter 42-storey companion tower containing the Park Hyatt hotel and branded residences.
notes: Kohn Pedersen Fox, 2017-23; 42 storeys, about 161 m (?). Coordinates offset by hand from the City Tower (?).
